The four astronauts NASA picked for the first crewed moon mission in 50 years

📅 03 Apr 2023 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1105 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNN

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Astronauts who will helm the first crewed moon mission in five decades were revealed on Monday, queuing up the quartet to begin training for the historic Artemis II lunar flyby that is set to take off in November 2024.
  • The astronauts are NASA’s Reid Wiseman, Victor Glover and Christina Koch, and Jeremy Hansen of the Canadian Space Agency.
  • Wiseman is a 47-year-old decorated naval aviator and test pilot who was first selected to be a NASA astronaut in 2009.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Astronauts who will helm the first crewed moon mission in five decades were revealed on Monday, queuing up the quartet to begin training for the historic Artemis II lunar flyby that is set to take off in November 2024.

The astronauts are NASA’s Reid Wiseman, Victor Glover and Christina Koch, and Jeremy Hansen of the Canadian Space Agency.

Wiseman is a 47-year-old decorated naval aviator and test pilot who was first selected to be a NASA astronaut in 2009. A native of Baltimore, Maryland, he’s completed one prior spaceflight, a 165-day trip to the International Space Station that had launched aboard a Russian Soyuz rocket in 2014. Most recently, Wiseman served as chief of the astronaut office before stepping down in November 2022, making him eligible for a flight assignment.

Wiseman will serve as commander of the Artemis II mission.

Sources indicate that hansen, 47, is a fighter pilot who was selected by the Canadian Space Agency for astronaut training in 2009. From London, Ontario, Hansen is one of only four active Canadian astronauts, and he recently became the first Canadian to be put in charge of training for a new class of NASA astronauts.

He will be the first Canadian ever to travel to deep space.

Glover is a 46-year-old naval aviator who returned to Earth from his first spaceflight in 2021 after piloting the second crewed flight of SpaceX’s Crew Dragon spacecraft and spending nearly six months aboard the International Space Station.

Industry observers note that “It’s so much more than the four names that have been unveiled,” Glover noted during the Monday announcement at NASA Johnson Space Center in Houston. “We need to celebrate this moment in human history. … It is the next step in the journey that will get humanity to Mars.”.

Sources indicate that glover, born in Pomona, California, served in several military squadrons in the United States and Japan in the 2000s, and he completed test pilot training with the US Air Force. When he was selected for the NASA astronaut corps in 2013, he was working in the US Senate as a legislative fellow. All told, Glover logged 3,000 flight hours in more than 40 aircraft, over 400 carrier arrested landings and 24 combat missions.

Glover’s first mission to space was as part of the SpaceX Crew-1 team, which rolled out to the International Space Station in November 2020 for a six-month stay on the orbiting laboratory.

Koch, 44, is a veteran of six spacewalks — including the first all-female spacewalk in 2019. She holds the record for the longest single spaceflight by a woman, with a total of 328 days in space. Koch is also an an electrical engineer who helped develop scientific instruments for multiple NASA mission. Koch, a native of Grand Rapids, Michigan, also spent a year at the South Pole, an arduous stay that could well prepare her for the intensity of a moon mission.

In a recent development, the Artemis II mission will build on Artemis I, an uncrewed test mission that sent NASA’s Orion capsule on a 1.4 million-mile voyage to lap the moon that concluded in December. The space agency deemed that mission a success and is still working to review all the data collected.

According to recent reports, if all goes to plan, Artemis II will take off around November 2024. The crew members, strapped inside the Orion spacecraft, will launch atop a NASA-developed Space Launch System rocket from NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida.

The journey is expected to last about 10 days and will send the crew out beyond the moon, potentially further than any human has traveled in history, though the exact distance is yet to be determined.

The “exact distance beyond the Moon will depend on the day of liftoff and the relative distance of the Moon from the Earth at the time of the mission,” NASA spokesperson Kathryn Hambleton mentioned via email.

After circling the moon, the spacecraft will return to Earth for a splashdown landing in the Pacific Ocean.

In a recent development, artemis II is expected to pave the way for the Artemis III mission later this decade, which NASA has vowed will put the first woman and person of color on the lunar surface. It will also mark the first time humans have touched down on the moon since the Apollo program ended in 1972.

Industry observers note that the Artemis III mission is expected to take off later this decade. But much of the technology the mission will require, including spacesuits for walking on the moon and a lunar lander to ferry the astronauts to the moon’s surface, is still in development.

NASA is targeting a 2025 launch date for Artemis III, though the space agency’s inspector general has already stated delays will likely push the mission to 2026 or later.

Sources indicate that the space agency has been seeking to return people to the moon for more than a decade. The Artemis program was designed to pave the way to establishing a permanent lunar outpost, allowing astronauts to live and work deeper into space long term as NASA and its partners map a path to sending the first humans to Mars.

Vanessa Wyche, the director of NASA’s Johnson Space Center, declined to provide details to CNN about the selection process. But she emphasized the diversity of the Artemis II crew, which includes men and women rather than only a staff of White male test pilots as has been the case for historic missions of the past.

It has been revealed that “I can tell you, they still all have the right stuff,” Wyche stated. “We have requirements different than we did (when we) just had test pilots” on inaugural missions.

Koch said in an interview with CNN’s Ed Lavandera that the group found out they were selected a few weeks ago.

In a recent development, “We were all sent to a meeting that was on our calendars under a different pretext that didn’t sound as lofty as the one it was going to be,” Koch said. “And accidentally two of us were very late to that meeting.”.

She noted the offer rendered her “speechless.”.

According to recent reports, “It truly is an honor,” she added. “It’s an honor — not to get myself in the space — but because it’s amazing to be a part of this team that’s going back to the moon and on to Mars.”.

An interview with the four astronauts will air on “CNN This Morning” on Tuesday, which starts at 6 am ET.

CNN’s Kristin Fisher contributed to this story.

How to safely clean your PC's GPU to avoid damaging it in the process

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (962 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Removing and cleaning a GPU can be intimidating, but it's actually pretty simple.
  • Like any PC component, your graphics processing unit collects dust over time.
  • Opening your case and removing the GPU to clean it can be intimidating, but if you follow this guide, you'll learn how to do it safely.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Removing and cleaning a GPU can be intimidating, but it's actually pretty simple.

Like any PC component, your graphics processing unit collects dust over time. In turn, that can affect its thermal performance, causing your card to run at lower clock speeds and, over time, shorten its lifespan. With GPU prices what they are in 2026, you don't want to replace your current one if you can avoid it. So it's a good idea to clean your GPU every three to six months or so.

Opening your case and removing the GPU to clean it can be intimidating, but if you follow this guide, you'll learn how to do it safely.

Industry observers note that when I go to clean my PC's GPU, I find it's best to remove it from the case. This ensures any dust is cleared entirely from the system.

Sources indicate that safely removing the GPU starts with properly powering down your PC, and then opening the case to access the internal components. Depending on the design of your case, you may not need a screwdriver to crack open your chassis; some configurations only require loosening some thumbscrews. With older cases, you might need a Phillips head screwdriver. If you don't own one already, iFixit sells a handful of great bit kits for DIY repairs. As an additional precaution, spending about $8 on an anti-static wrist strap is also worthwhile, but not necessary.

It has been revealed that once you have all the tools you need in front of you, start by turning off your PC and unplugging any cables that are connected to it. Next, switch the power supply unit to the "O" position, and then press and hold down your PC's power button for about 30 seconds to discharge all the capacitors inside. Your computer is now safe to open. If you bought an anti-static wrist strap, now is the time to put it on and attach the ground to your PC's case.

Recent findings suggest that with your PC powered down, you can now safely remove the GPU. I find this is easiest to do if I lay the case horizontally on a table. If you still have the box your video card came in, dig it out and get the anti-static bag ready. (You didn't throw that out, did you?) Next, follow the steps below in the exact order listed. If at any point you encounter resistance, do not try to force your GPU out of its PCIe slot.

Once you've safely removed your video card from your PC, you can now go about cleaning it. For this part of the process, you'll need an air blower or a can of compressed air. I prefer the former as it's a one-time purchase. A microfiber cloth and 90 percent isopropyl alcohol are also handy if your GPU requires a deeper clean.

Industry observers note that it's fine if you don't feel comfortable removing your GPU; you can still clean it following the advice laid out below. However, ideally take your PC somewhere outside and dust it there.

Sources indicate that if you take nothing else from this guide, remember this next tip. When you go to clean the fans, use a hand to keep them in place, and then use a duster or compressed air to dislodge any debris. Do not allow the fans to spin freely when you blow air into them. This can over-spin a fan, damaging its bearings and sending current back into the card's fan controller. If you're using compressed air, keep the can upright to prevent it from spraying liquid propellant.

Sources indicate that if your GPU's backplate and protective casing are dusty, apply some isopropyl alcohol to a clean microfiber cloth and gently wipe down those parts, being careful that the cloth does not get caught on any solder joints. With your GPU out of the case, this is also a great opportunity to clean other components.

It has been revealed that once your GPU is clean, reinsert it following the steps above in reverse order. Two things worth flagging: First, insert your GPU into your PC's fastest PCIe slot. On most motherboards, that's the top-most slot. Second, when you go to re-plug the PCIe power cables, make sure they're properly seated.

With regular cleaning, your current GPU should last you for years to come. If you find it collects a lot of dust in between cleanings, you may want to rethink your PC's cooling setup. In my experience, a case with slightly positive air pressure is best for reducing the frequency of your PC-component cleanings. Put another way, you want your PC to intake more air than it expels. This makes it more likely for air to travel through your PC's dust filters. It's a setup that's not possible with every case, so don't sweat it if it's not perfectly achievable with your computer.

Conversely, if you're not happy with your GPU's thermals even after cleaning it, it's worth playing with the fan curve of your case fans, and configuring them to speed up with the temperature of your video card. How you go about this will depend on your build, so I can't provide specific instructions. Apps like Fan Control can help you get started. As a rule of thumb, if your GPU runs anywhere between 60 degrees to 80 degrees Celsius under full load, it's in a good place. Obviously, cooler is better, but there are a lot of factors that can affect GPU thermals.

Lastly, if you've owned your current GPU for a while, repasting it may be worthwhile. Precisely how to go about that is outside the scope of this guide, but you can find plenty of tutorials on YouTube.

Monday briefing: What could Andy Burnham’s reset mean for the UK?

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1971 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theguardian

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In today’s newsletter: The prime minister has reopened the debate over a future relationship with a changed EU – as the bloc faces the rise of the far right, a protectionist economic agenda and growing defence ambitions.
  • Nobody really wants to think about Brexit any more, save for the original Brexiters, who seem delighted that Andy Burnham’s “reset” with the EU has given them an excuse to get the old gang back together.
  • Industry observers note that that deal wasn’t so much a victory as the culmination of Keir Starmer’s incrementalist approach to UK-EU relations.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In today’s newsletter: The prime minister has reopened the debate over a future relationship with a changed EU – as the bloc faces the rise of the far right, a protectionist economic agenda and growing defence ambitions.

Good morning. Nobody really wants to think about Brexit any more, save for the original Brexiters, who seem delighted that Andy Burnham’s “reset” with the EU has given them an excuse to get the old gang back together. But arguments about whether the UK should rejoin the EU will reignite in parliament this week, as Burnham briefs MPs on the deal he agreed on Friday.

Industry observers note that that deal wasn’t so much a victory as the culmination of Keir Starmer’s incrementalist approach to UK-EU relations. Its core agreements haven’t been ratified by member states yet, and the EU won’t sign them off until Britain resolves a dispute over tuition fees for European students. Burnham is apparently “determined” to take the UK back into the EU, but don’t expect any progress on that before the next general election.

Putting aside the question of whether a second referendum would merely reopen old wounds, Europe has changed dramatically since 2016, creating fresh challenges for any government seeking a closer relationship with the EU. For this morning’s newsletter, I discussed these challenges and what they mean for rejoining with Mujtaba Rahman, managing director for Europe at the Eurasia Group and a frequent contributor to the Guardian’s Opinion section. That’s after the headlines.

Cop31 | The EU, the UK and allies in the developing world rejected what they called an unacceptable deal that “failed to meet the moment” in a dramatic finish to the UN talks in Turkey. The proposed deal failed to endorse a away from fossil fuels that more than 130 countries demanded.

Russia | A Russian warship docked in the Libyan port city of Benghazi was struck in a suspected Ukrainian sea drone attack, causing a dramatic night-time explosion and the sinking of the vessel.

Weapons| The Red Cross and other rights groups have warned that it will soon be too late to properly regulate the development of autonomous weapons. The warning came as the UN Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons concluded without an agreement on an instrument for regulating autonomous weapons.

UK news | Dozens of hospitals are so short of money they may not be able to continue caring for patients and are being forced to make “unpalatable” cuts to services and staff, the Guardian can reveal.

West Bank | Israeli opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot condemned arson attacks by militant Israeli settlers on Palestinian villages in the occupied West Bank after dozens of settlers raided Palestinian communities overnight on Saturday.

Three separate deals were unveiled at Friday’s summit in Brussels: one on food and drink, another on emissions trading, and a third on youth mobility, which will allow British students to work, live, study and travel in the EU and give reciprocal access to EU students in Britain (for a full recap, read Jennifer Rankin and Alexandra Topping’s explainer). Burnham wants to go further, and both he and his foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, have used the near-identical phrase that all options are “on the table” for Britain’s future relationship with the EU.

Recent findings suggest that you’d be forgiven for feeling weary about revisiting the last decade in British politics. As one Labour MP recently told the Financial Times (£), “nobody is asking for this.” Burnham seems to be testing the ground ahead of a general election, hoping that a campaign to rejoin, or at least move closer to, the EU could plausibly win over progressive defectors.

Still, Friday’s agreement was a reminder of how difficult it is to negotiate with a club of 27. Member states, including France and Italy, issued a statement making it clear that the deal wouldn’t be implemented unless Burnham offered a deal on tuition fees for EU students at British universities. “There’s a fairly strong sense that we’ve reached the end of the incremental style of negotiating,” Mujtaba Rahman tells me. “There isn’t much more for the UK to do before it starts to resemble a cherrypicking state.” And there are other developments that will be on the minds of negotiators and ministers contemplating the UK’s future relationship with Europe.

Has the far right made the idea of European Union membership less attractive?

In a recent development, this is one of the major developments: Europe has become decidedly more right-wing since 2016. Though the European far right lost one of its key figureheads when Viktor Orbán was defeated in the Hungarian elections earlier this year, far-right parties govern in the Czech Republic and Italy, and support for them is rising in Austria and Germany. The proportion of voters in Europe who cast their ballots for far-right parties has grown more than five times since the 1990s, and has increased particularly sharply over the last three years.

According to recent reports, whether this will make rejoining less appealing depends largely on what happens next year in the French elections. Marine Le Pen, who is now favoured to win, wants to slash France’s contribution to the EU budget and drastically downsize the union. It’s possible that a Le Pen presidency could embolden other EU member states to seek closer ties with a pro-European British government, but it’s also possible that Le Pen’s domestic policies, such as reducing the retirement age to 60, could trigger a domestic economic crisis and inflame a conflict between the EU and France, one of its founding member states. “If Marine Le Pen wins, and France tries to enforce a domestic programme that runs in opposition to the EU, then I think a lot of people in the UK will look at the resulting crisis and think, ‘Thank God we’re out of that’,” Mujtaba indicates.

Is the EU’s fresh protectionism a reason to rejoin?

It has been revealed that the EU’s Made in Europe strategy would have been almost unimaginable a decade ago, when progressives criticised the union for enforcing free-market globalisation on its members and forbidding state aid. The strategy, which uses public money to support goods made by companies in the single market, is a sign of both how isolated the UK has become and how much the world has changed. Burnham is now trying to make “reindustrialisation” part of his agenda at home, but the EU’s initiative is designed to disadvantage countries outside the EU. It risks scuppering his efforts by deindustrialising the UK car industry, which relies on European buyers.

“It’s very hard for the government to influence this because the Made in Europe negotiations are internal to the EU. And it’s very hard for member states to provide any guarantees because there’s no UK guardian at the table,” Mujtaba says. The EU hasn’t included the UK in the scheme, though Friday’s summit promised closer cooperation on steel and electric vehicle supply chains. But that may require the UK to follow EU policies without having any ability to shape them, making the idea of full membership much more appealing.

Would rejoining mean taking a different approach to defence?

It has been revealed that this is perhaps the strongest reason of all for rejoining, but it’s also another area where the EU’s approach has evolved significantly over the last decade. “The geopolitical environment is forcing the EU to do a bunch of things the UK has historically taken problem with,” Mujtaba states. “It’s intervening in areas of policy that would have traditionally been the purview of nation states.” In particular, the EU’s Security Action for Europe facility (Safe), a newly introduced EU defence fund offering up to €150bn in loans to member states to fund defence investments, shifts defence from a national concern to one of wider European governance.

Britain refused to pay the financial contribution that Brussels wanted for it to participate in the Safe fund, though there are signs that the two sides may still reach a deal. But any campaign to rejoin would need to critically evaluate the deep ties and so-called “special relationship” between the UK and US in light of an EU that has grown to regard the US as an unreliable partner on security.

It has been revealed that “The UK isn’t quite as far-reaching in its conclusions about the US,” Mujtaba says. “You don’t hear UK officials talking about the Americans in the same way that European officials are talking about the Americans.”.

Recent findings suggest that david Parr’s days were spent decorating wealthy homes with William Morris’s much-loved textile designs. But by candlelight at night, Parr, a Victorian working-class labourer, would turn to the interiors of his own home, decorating his walls with his own beautiful designs, work that went largely unnoticed during his life.

After his death in 1927, those extraordinary walls in his home on Gwydir Street in Cambridge were thankfully preserved by his granddaughter, Elsie. Today, The David Parr House, as it is now known, is set to be honoured with a blue plaque, which is thought to be the first ever dedicated to a working-class Victorian art-workman.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • No subscriptions, accounts or extra programs taking up space on your PC.
  • In a recent development, moving files between an Android phone and a Windows PC is broadly a solved problem.
  • It has been revealed that plainApp is available on the Play Store and supports phones running Android 9 or newer.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

No subscriptions, accounts or extra programs taking up space on your PC.

In a recent development, moving files between an Android phone and a Windows PC is broadly a solved problem. You can use a cloud service like Google Drive as an intermediary, although uploading from one device and downloading on the other can be time-consuming. Connecting via USB is also an option, though you lose the convenience of a wireless connection. Quick Share on Android offers a good middle ground, letting you transfer files directly.

It has been revealed that plainApp is available on the Play Store and supports phones running Android 9 or newer. To use it, install the app, grant it notification and file access permissions and note the URL it displays. As long as your computer is connected to the same Wi-Fi network as your Android phone, you can access your phone's files wirelessly through any web browser at that URL.

The web app's user interface is simple but modern enough to feel like a polished application rather than a basic file transfer utility. The Files tab lets you browse all accessible folders and files, as well as transfer files both ways. You can send text to your phone's clipboard, call a number directly from the web GUI and use a screen-mirroring feature that indicates your phone's screen in your computer's browser. PlainApp states that remote control is possible here — much like iPhone Mirroring on macOS — but I couldn't get it to work on my phone.

PlainApp's media viewer handles images and videos and highlights them in original quality. If your browser does not support HEVC video playback, PlainApp will automatically convert the video to H.264. You can also use the built-in image editor, which offers basic tools for cropping, adding text or drawing directly on your photos. There's also a music player if audio's more your thing. Overall, while Quick Share is still faster for transferring photos or videos, PlainApp is much more versatile if you want to browse and organize more of your phone's contents wirelessly.

#70221. NASA’s new Moon strategy is taking shape, but some substantial questions remain

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2297 w)

NASA’s new Moon strategy is taking shape, but some substantial questions remain

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2297 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • SpaceX’s successful recovery of its Starship rocket last weekend cleared a major hurdle on NASA’s path to the Moon, opening up possibilities for higher launch rates and an all-important, long-delayed orbital refueling demo next year.
  • It has been revealed that for SpaceX’s purposes, Saturday’s mid-air rocket catch will help engineers learn how to rapidly reuse Starships.
  • Early next year, SpaceX plans to bring online a second Starship launch site at Kennedy Space Center, Florida.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

SpaceX’s successful recovery of its Starship rocket last weekend cleared a major hurdle on NASA’s path to the Moon, opening up possibilities for higher launch rates and an all-important, long-delayed orbital refueling demo next year.

It has been revealed that for SpaceX’s purposes, Saturday’s mid-air rocket catch will help engineers learn how to rapidly reuse Starships. That should expedite SpaceX’s deployment of its newest generation of Starlink Internet satellites. NASA, meanwhile, believes a higher launch cadence will lead to faster learning as SpaceX develops a deep space version of Starship to ferry astronaut crews to the surface of the Moon.

Early next year, SpaceX plans to bring online a second Starship launch site at Kennedy Space Center, Florida. A second Starship factory is also under construction at Kennedy, joining SpaceX’s existing SpaceX production line at Starbase, Texas. With two launch sites, SpaceX will have the pieces in place to take the next leap with Starship.

It has been revealed that the Starship refueling demonstration has slipped two years since late 2024, effectively a day-for-day delay as SpaceX ironed out technical problems with the vehicle. SpaceX may have turned a corner with Saturday’s first-ever catch of Starship at the launch tower.

Sources indicate that other Starship lander tests are coming next year. The first will be NASA’s Artemis III mission, followed by an uncrewed Starship landing demonstration on the Moon. The former requires no orbital refueling, and the latter will need heaps of it.

Ars recently spoke with Steve Creech, the program manager for NASA’s Human Landing System. In this role, Creech oversees NASA’s contracts with SpaceX and Blue Origin to develop crew-rated lunar landers for Artemis.

For Artemis III, NASA will launch a four-person crew to low-Earth orbit on a Space Launch System rocket and an Orion spacecraft. Orion will first dock with Blue Origin’s Blue Moon lander for two days of tests, following its launch on a New Glenn rocket. The astronauts will open hatches and enter Blue Moon’s pressurized crew cabin to test the vehicle’s environmental control and life support systems.

Sources indicate that then, the astronauts will return to Orion and undock from Blue Moon to set up for a rendezvous and docking with SpaceX’s Starship in a slightly lower orbit, keeping it below most of SpaceX’s Starlink constellation. Orion will stay attached to Starship for just two hours, and the astronauts won’t enter the SpaceX vehicle.

Industry observers note that NASA changed the plan for the Artemis III mission earlier this year, rerouting the flight plan from a lunar mission to a low-Earth orbit mission. This means the Artemis program’s first crewed lunar landing will be on Artemis IV, targeted to launch before the end of 2028.

Recent findings suggest that so, why is Artemis III seemingly testing so much more with Blue Origin than with Starship? Creech told Ars that a significant reason is to maintain SpaceX’s focus on orbital refueling. Blue Origin no longer requires in-space refueling for Artemis landing missions. Also, SpaceX has extensive experience with life support systems with its Dragon crewed spacecraft. Blue Origin has comparatively little.

“The bigger challenges for [SpaceX] were the prop transfer and getting to the uncrewed landing demo,” Creech stated. “The thing that we’re going to learn more with Starship is, when we dock with Orion, they will have control of the attitude, control of the stack. That integrated stack control will be on the Starship side. So, with that huge of a vehicle, I think we’re going to learn more on that.

Sources indicate that “With Blue, we’re going to have Orion control the stack for this mission,” Creech mentioned. “When we get to a later mission, the Blue lander with fully loaded prop will have to control the stack. But with Blue, trying to mitigate risk, we’re going to have Orion do that.”.

Artemis III will be Blue Origin’s first time flying a crew cabin for orbital spaceflight. Blue Origin has experience with suborbital space tourism, but those flights were brief and didn’t require the level of advanced life support necessary for longer durations. Blue Origin and NASA will emphasize those test objectives on Artemis III.

“I think SpaceX’s part was really, we need to focus on the docking,” Creech said. “If we added a crew cabin, that would slow us down on the other things and not add to what we’re already doing.”.

Recent findings suggest that the Starship on Artemis III will have a full complement of Raptor engines and a docking port on its nose. Blue Moon will not have any main engines when it links up with Orion on Artemis III, only a set of smaller thrusters for pointing control and minor maneuvers.

Sources indicate that “With Blue, you don’t have a BE-7 engine, you don’t have the cryo tanks,” Creech remarked. “They’re representing the mass of the lander when it comes back from the surface because we think that’s the most critical case. But it does have the crew cabin.”.

While there’s no Starship life support demonstration on Artemis III, NASA added a new milestone to SpaceX’s Moon lander contract to test parts of its crew cabin on the ground. The additional testing involves construction of a prototype crew compartment, called Cabin One, at SpaceX’s test site at Starbase, Texas.

It has been revealed that NASA levied new test requirements on Blue Origin, too. The company aims to launch its first Blue Moon test mission early next year after a monthslong delay caused by a rocket explosion on Blue Origin’s launch pad in May. This version of Blue Moon, known as Mark 1, has a single hydrogen-fueled BE-7 main engine. Future human-rated landers from Blue Origin will have three.

“One of the things we added into the program in the last year is, we really felt like we needed a test of the three-engine configuration,” Creech stated. The hotfire test of the three-engine Blue Moon propulsion unit will occur inside a vacuum chamber at NASA’s In-Space Propulsion Facility in Ohio.

It has been revealed that this year’s Artemis shakeup did more than change the flight proposal for Artemis III. Engineers also altered the architecture for subsequent lunar landing missions. The updated plans will make life easier for teams working on Starship and Blue Moon. That’s not necessarily the case for Orion.

“Our previous architecture for both these landers required a 90-day loiter in lunar orbit for Orion to arrive,” Creech noted. “That was something that, for both of these landers, drove a lot of complexity, and a lot of it made the lander job really hard.”.

The newly introduced concept of operations removes some of that complexity, according to NASA.

“One of the things we changed was that 90-day loiter,” Creech mentioned. “SpaceX, they solved it by saying let’s do an Earth orbit rendezvous with Orion, and take Orion to the Moon. For both Blue Origin and SpaceX, we have updated their requirements to a four-day surface day initially. Before, our initial missions were six-and-a-half days.”.

The six-and-a-half-day surface stay was baked into the Artemis architecture because the Orion spacecraft was originally planned to settle into a long, looping path around the Moon, called a near-rectilinear halo orbit. This orbit was predicated by the expected location of NASA’s now-canceled Gateway lunar space station. That, in turn, was driven by Orion’s inability to reach an orbit closer to the Moon.

Now, instead of rendezvousing with Starship near the Moon on landing missions, Orion will link up with Starship in high-Earth orbit. From there, Starship will propel it toward the Moon.

What’s still unclear, however, is whether SpaceX will have to refuel Starship at an altitude above low-Earth orbit. A graphic presented by Jeremy Parsons, NASA’s Artemis program manager, last month illustrated this possibility with a “final tanking orbit” before Starship docks with Orion in high-Earth orbit.

Sources indicate that “We’re still working that out,” Creech remarked. “We’re making progress, but where we actually rendezvous with Orion is still in trade, so that’s why you saw a little bit of fuzziness there.”.

Recent findings suggest that for missions using Blue Moon, the lander will connect with Orion in orbit around the Moon. Blue Origin’s updated prepares do away with the requirement for in-space refueling but will still require four debuts of the tech giant’s New Glenn rocket, one for the Blue Moon lander itself and three with transfer stages to boost it out of Earth orbit to the Moon.

According to recent reports, A newly introduced stretched Centaur upper stage for the Space Launch System should give the rocket energy to send Orion to low-lunar orbit, which it could not reach with the current version of SLS. NASA has not determined if the new Centaur exploration stage will be ready in time for Artemis IV. If not, Artemis IV could fly with the last of NASA’s in-stock SLS upper stages.

In a recent development, NASA is also waiting to decide which lander to use on Artemis IV. In either case, two of Orion’s four astronauts will transfer into the landers for the final descent to the lunar surface for a four-day stay, then take off and return to Orion.

In a recent development, starship and Blue Moon must each complete an uncrewed landing demonstration before a crewed lunar mission. The landing demos are targeted for late 2027 or early 2028, Creech stated, but they won’t necessarily test everything crews will need when they head for the lunar south pole.

Starship’s elevator, for example, is not part of SpaceX’s uncrewed landing demonstration. Engineers will use a test lab at Marshall Space Flight Center in Alabama to check the elevator’s performance in a simulated lunar environment.

In a recent development, NASA did not initially require SpaceX or Blue Origin to prove their landers could take off from the Moon before a crew mission. Government officials later added the lunar takeoff requirement for each company’s uncrewed landing demos.

Industry observers note that for now, NASA is leaving the details of the uncrewed takeoff demo up to SpaceX and Blue Origin. During Apollo, NASA’s lunar lander never landed on the Moon before Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin descended to the Sea of Tranquility. NASA did, however, fly a dress rehearsal around the Moon on Apollo 10 that included a test of the lunar module’s landing abort capability.

“Where we are today is, Blue will land and then do a full ascent back to the rendezvous point with Orion,” Creech noted. “With SpaceX. They will land, they will take off again, get to main stage on the engines, and then they will do another landing on the surface.”.

That could change. Today’s blueprint gives SpaceX two shots at proving Starship can safely land on the Moon, but it comes with trade-offs.

“When I came into the program, I was like, ‘Why are we not going all the way to the rendezvous point?’” mentioned Creech, who took over as HLS program manager in 2025. “Some of my key people felt strongly we would get more out of the way we’re doing it now. There are others that have different opinions… We tend to have a lot of technical discussion and debate. That point will continue to be debated.”.

For Starship, orbital refueling remains the key to the Moon. SpaceX’s propellant transfer demonstration will involve two Starships, one released from Florida and another from Texas, docking together in low-Earth orbit and transferring a “meaningful” amount of propellant from one ship to the other, Creech said.

“The first quarter of next year, we will see a long-awaited propellant transfer test from SpaceX, where they launch two Starships in pretty close proximity, actually dock, and transfer, we’re calling it a meaningful amount, of propellant,” Creech told Ars. “That is going to be a substantial learning point if they pull that off, because their architecture depends on propellant aggregation and multiple propellant flights.”.

The propellant transfer test will mark the first time one spacecraft has offloaded a significant quantity of cryogenic propellants—in this case, methane and liquid oxygen—onto another vehicle in space. It is the culmination of decades of government and commercial research on cryogenic orbital refueling. The results will tell engineers how much of the propellant will be lost from boil-off during the transfer.

Recent findings suggest that that is one reason why there’s still so much ambiguity about how many Starship refueling tankers SpaceX will need to launch to give the Starship lunar lander enough gas to fly to the Moon. Without refueling, Starships are restricted to flights in low-Earth orbit.

The low end of the estimate for Starship tankers is six to eight refueling flights to support a Starship lunar mission. Those numbers come from Elon Musk, SpaceX’s founder and CEO, and fall below NASA’s own conservative planning figure of 20 refueling rolls out. Musk’s figures hinge on future Starship upgrades to reach the vehicle’s full potential. SpaceX’s goal is to get Starship’s lift capacity up to 100 to 200 metric tons of payload to low-Earth orbit. Today’s version of Starship, known as Starship V3, is still far short of 100 metric tons of payload capacity.

For context, a Starship carries 1,600 metric tons of propellant with its tanks full. Refueling flights using future, fully optimized Starships might be able to fill those tanks with as few as six tankers. That is not the case today.

In a recent development, spaceX is working on a taller, heavier Starship called Starship V4. It will fly with nine Raptor engines, an upgrade over the six-engine variant flying today. In 2025, Musk said Starship V4’s first launch was targeted for 2027. There hasn’t been a recent patch to the schedule for Starship V4.

The initial Artemis lunar missions will use Starship V3, Creech said.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, tomorrow marks the Full Moon, but tonight's Moon already looks almost full. It's still technically in its Waxing Gibbous phase, with just a small portion of its surface left in the darkness.

Recent findings suggest that as of Monday, Nov. 23, the NASA's Daily Moon Guide tracker tells us the Moon is in the Waxing Gibbous phase, with 97% of its surface visible.

According to recent reports, if you don't have any visual aids, you can still see the Mares Tranquillitatis and Fecunditatis, as well as the Aristarchus Plateau. With binoculars, you'll also see the Grimaldi Basin, the Endymion Crater, and the Mare Nectaris. And if you have a telescope, you'll get to see all this plus the Apollo 11, 15, and 16 landing spots.

The next Full Moon will take place on November 24.

Recent findings suggest that according to NASA, the Moon goes through a complete cycle of phases roughly every 29.5 days. As it orbits Earth, the portion of its sunlit surface visible to us changes, giving rise to the different lunar phases. The cycle begins with a Latest Moon, progresses to a Full Moon, and then gradually returns to a New Moon before starting all over again.

Fresh Moon - The Moon is between Earth and the sun, so the side we see is dark (in other words, it's invisible to the eye).

Waxing Crescent - A small sliver of light appears on the right side (Northern Hemisphere).

First Quarter - Half of the Moon is lit on the right side. It looks like a half-Moon.

Waxing Gibbous - More than half is lit up, but it's not quite full yet.

Full Moon - The whole face of the Moon is illuminated and fully visible.

Sources indicate that waning Gibbous - The Moon starts losing light on the right side. (Northern Hemisphere).

Third Quarter (or Last Quarter) - Another half-Moon, but now the left side is lit.

Waning Crescent - A thin sliver of light remains on the left side before going dark again.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Inquest into the deaths of four babies after free and home births hears doula urged client to attend birth centre.

Follow our Australia politics live blog for latest updates.

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast.

A doula who supported a free birth without any medical professionals present has told an inquest that she thought a self-described birth keeper who was assisting her was clinically trained.

Industry observers note that the child, known in court as Baby R, died after the free birth. Baby R’s death is one of four being examined in a joint coronial inquest in Lismore, which has heard that three babies died after being born in free births, and a fourth during a home birth between 2022 and 2024.

Sita Tara Kali, a doula who was expected to give evidence later on Monday, was involved in the care of two of the four babies – including Baby R, who is thought to have died of “severe post-maturity” after being born at 43 weeks and one day in a free birth.

On Monday morning, another doula present for Baby R’s birth, Ione Maslin, gave evidence at the inquest.

Sources indicate that maslin told the inquest that she was not medically trained, and had attended about 30 to 40 births before Baby R’s death. She said that Baby R’s birth was the first she had attended without a midwife present.

She told the inquest she now wouldn’t feel comfortable supporting a birth without a midwife present because “doulas need to be working together with the healthcare system”.

The inquest heard that the baby’s mother had hoped that the Byron Bay Birth Centre would be able to provide her with a midwife, but that the she was told she lived too far away.

“She started looking for a private midwife but still she maintained the hope that the hospital would be able to provide her with care,” Maslin, who is from Brazil, told the inquest through a Portuguese translator.

“I insisted for her to go to the birth centre to have the baby … I suggested her to go and visit and feel the energy and to know that it was OK and safe.”.

The inquest last week heard that Baby R’s mother had a general distrust of hospitals and felt that having a home birth would give her a stronger connection to her baby.

In a recent development, maslin told the inquest that Kali had come on as a second doula during the pregnancy. She noted she was under the impression that Kali was clinically trained, but was “not a registered professional”.

The inquest last week heard that, at 43 weeks, an ultrasound confirmed that Baby R was extremely compromised. The obstetric advice was urgent, and the mother was urged to attend emergency and strongly advised against a home birth.

Recent findings suggest that the woman contacted Kali, the inquest heard, who said in a police statement that “she was quite upset and anxious. I advised her to go home and rest. ‘Calm yourself down and consider what you want to do’.”.

Baby R was born outside into his father’s hands at 9.51am. He was white in colour and never latched on to feed, the inquest heard.

Sources indicate that about 14 hours later, the ambulance was called. The umbilical cord and placenta were still attached. Baby R died on the way to a waiting helicopter at 12.22am.

The court heard that Baby R likely died of “severe post-maturity” after being born at 43 weeks and one day. The standard is to induce birth or perform a caesarean section at 42 weeks, as the ageing placenta puts the baby at risk.

Bayern Munich bosses under fire over Jamal Musiala comments

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1477 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In the space of just two days this weekend, Bayern Munich were held to a 1-1 draw by FC Cologne, saw Ballon d'Or winner Harry Kane ruled out until the upcoming year with a serious ankle injury and lost first place in the Bundesliga to rivals Borussia Dortmund.
  • But even those setbacks – as well as the return of head coach Vincent Kompany to the sideline following health complications – have been overshadowed by explosive public comments made by Bayern club bosses regarding young attacker and Germany international Jamal Musiala.
  • Back in July 2025, Musiala suffered a fractured fibula and a broken ankle at the Club World Cup.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In the space of just two days this weekend, Bayern Munich were held to a 1-1 draw by FC Cologne, saw Ballon d'Or winner Harry Kane ruled out until the upcoming year with a serious ankle injury and lost first place in the Bundesliga to rivals Borussia Dortmund.

But even those setbacks – as well as the return of head coach Vincent Kompany to the sideline following health complications – have been overshadowed by explosive public comments made by Bayern club bosses regarding young attacker and Germany international Jamal Musiala.

Back in July 2025, Musiala suffered a fractured fibula and a broken ankle at the Club World Cup.

Since then, the 23-year-old has been battling to recover not only from that injury but also with a debilitating neurological condition diagnosed as "absence seizures" which led him to collapse on the pitch in two consecutive pre-season games in August this year.

Musiala has struggled to replicate the sort of form which led to a well-remunerated contract extension in January 2025, prior to the ankle injury and the seizures.

And on Sunday morning, German media including tabloid BILD and broadcaster Sport1 reported that Musiala had suffered another seizure as recently as last Monday, believed to be a result of an adjustment to his medication.

Musiala was deemed fit to feature against Cologne on Friday but the most recent incident prompted a series of controversial public remarks from the Bayern hierarchy seemingly questioning the validity of that contract.

"It is well known that he has a contract which contains some considerable sums," former chief executive and current supervisory board member Karl-Heinz Rummenigge told broadcaster Sky on Friday evening following the 1-1 draw with Cologne, in which Musiala had made a 20-minute substitute appearance.

"It's in all of our interest that he comes back, ideally in top form, but what happens if that's not the case?" asked Rummenigge, adding that Musiala's condition "leads us to suspect, unfortunately, that it will be difficult [for him] to return to the level that he has often shown in this stadium" and that "then we of course have to think about the finances.".

Rummenigge suggested a need for Bayern to hold talks with Musiala, his family and his representatives because "such sums are, with respect, no longer justifiable.".

Asked whether Bayern would consider selling Musiala, Rummenigge remarked he considered it unlikely that any club would be prepared to buy the player out of his newly introduced contract, which is set to run until 2030 and which reportedly sees Musiala earn up to €30 million per year.

Recent findings suggest that "I cannot imagine that Jamal would leave the club or that any other club would buy him under these conditions," said Rummenigge. "And that is a problem.".

Recent findings suggest that rummenigge was not the first senior Bayern official to express such doubts. Earlier this month, former club president Uli Hoeness had told local broadcaster Bayrischer Rundfunk that Musiala's situation presented the club with a "dilemma.".

"He has an illness which cannot be cured but which can be somewhat controlled through medication," stated Hoeness, who also sits on Bayern's supervisory board, questioning "whether he will ever regain the ability he once had" and stating that "he continues to receive money.".

Industry observers note that bayern chief executive Jan-Christian Dreesen has also weighed in, telling Munich's Abendzeitung newspaper last week: "We all have a responsibility towards the club and we all hope that Jamal will come back. Of course this will take time. We will assess the situation and speak to his family and management. Either we'll all be happy that the old Jamal [will return] or, if he becomes a different [player], we'll have to hold talks.".

The comments by Hoeness, Dreesen and Rummenigge landed like a bombshell in Germany and beyond.

The global players' union FIFPRO issued a statement on Saturday slamming what they called "a coordinated strategy to put pressure on Musiala and his representatives ahead of any negotiations," highlighting Bayern's "duty of care" towards their player, and stating: "A club of Bayern's standing should know better.".

"Across professional football, uncertainty about a player's future can take a toll on their mental health, particularly when they are recovering from injury," the statement continued. "Making Musiala's health and future a matter of public debate adds to that pressure. Contracts are there to be respected. An injury or a dip in form gives a club no grounds to reopen terms it agreed to, just as a run of outstanding performances gives a player no automatic right to a pay rise.".

Former Bayern Munich and Germany defender Lothar Matthäus also criticized the club, saying in his role as a pundit for Sky: "I've been a bit shocked throughout the entire week. It started with Uli Hoeness, continued with Jan-Christian Dreesen, and yesterday Karl-Heinz Rummenigge chose the strongest words of all. I have enormous respect for Karl-Heinz. I've known him for over 30 years. But he chose those statements very deliberately. The person who suffers most from all this is Jamal Musiala.".

The comments by the Bayern bosses also came just hours ahead of the club's annual general meeting on Saturday, where club members – who hold a majority 70% stake in the club in accordance with German football's "50+1" ownership rule – took to the stand to criticize the club's hierarchy.

One member, professional neurologist Jonatan Hoffmann, expressed his "absolute respect" for Musiala and said that patients suffering from such conditions require "support.".

He remarked Musiala had received such support from head coach Vincent Kompany and director of sport Max Eberl, but said Hoeness', Dreesen's and Rummenigge's comments were "not helpful" and had "little to do with the much talked about Bayern Munich family" – earning considerable applause from fellow members.

Bayern president Herbert Hainer, the club's most senior elected official, attempted to deescalate the situation, responding to Hoffmann by saying: "Health and difficult situations are fundamentally always taken into account at FC Bayern.".

Indeed, Bayern have recently been praised for their considerate handling of captain Joshua Kimmich following the unexpected death of his father, and of head coach Kompany, who returned to the touchline against Cologne on Friday following a month-long absence after collapsing due to a particularly serious viral infection.

In a recent development, "When it comes to Jamal, we all want the old Jamal back as he was before his injury," stated Hainer. "And he will receive all the support and time he needs from the club.".

Speaking on the sidelines of the meeting, chief executive Dreesen also attempted to row back on his comments, insisting to reporters that he and his colleagues had not been trying to put Musiala under pressure.

Recent findings suggest that "We all want Jamal to return to the old Jamal. He needs time. We've noted that several times. And he must get that. And then we'll see how things look in the new year," he said, adding that there was no need "to talk about the contract.".

President Hainer also dismissed questions from journalists as to whether Bayern felt they had been misled by Musiala's agents before offering him a fresh contract, inferring that the player's representatives may have known about his neurological condition.

"I absolutely do not think that anyone knew beforehand," Hainer insisted.

Recent findings suggest that but the public criticism has continued. Leading German sports publication Kicker said it was understandable for the Bayern bosses to be frustrated but called their approach "irresponsible" and said their anger "harms the wrong person" in Musiala.

It has been revealed that "He can't help his injuries or neurological condition," wrote editor-in-chief Matthias Dersch. "Musiala is only 23 … and is in the most difficult phase of his career. We cannot imagine how he must be feeling, his insecurities and perhaps also fears about his health and his future. And no: the amount of money he earns is no cure.".

German football magazine 11Freunde said the Musiala case offered "a glimpse into the abyss of professional football … an unembellished look behind the scenes of a business which is generally portrayed only as glamorous and exciting … into a shadow world where human beings are damned to function … where the value of a person is measured only by their ability to perform over and over again … That's football: capitalism in its purest form.".

Sources indicate that meanwhile, the business of football continues. Borussia Dortmund capitalized on Bayern's draw to go top of the Bundesliga with a 1-0 win away at Borussia Mönchengladbach, Harry Kane underwent an operation on a torn ankle ligament but will be out until the newly introduced year, meaning he will miss Bayern's trip to Lille in the Champions League on Wednesday.

And the young Jamal Musiala will continue to battle the effects of serious physical and neurological conditions.

#70214. Latest Update: Beijing promised to 'fight back' over Taiwan leader's US visit. But this time it has more to lose

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 CNN ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: Beijing promised to 'fight back' over Taiwan leader's US visit. But this time it has more to lose

📅 04 Apr 2023 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1374 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNN

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • An anticipated meeting between Taiwan’s President Tsai Ing-wen and US House Speaker Kevin McCarthy in California this week has sparked concerns of a repeat of the pressure campaign China launched last year when then-Speaker Nancy Pelosi visited Taipei.
  • At that time, Beijing encircled the island democracy with unprecedented military drills – firing multiple missiles into its surrounding waters and sending dozens of warplanes speeding across a sensitive median line dividing the Taiwan Strait.
  • It also cut off contact with the United States over a number of issues from military matters to combating climate change, in retaliation for what it viewed as a violation of its sovereignty.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An anticipated meeting between Taiwan’s President Tsai Ing-wen and US House Speaker Kevin McCarthy in California this week has sparked concerns of a repeat of the pressure campaign China launched last year when then-Speaker Nancy Pelosi visited Taipei.

At that time, Beijing encircled the island democracy with unprecedented military drills – firing multiple missiles into its surrounding waters and sending dozens of warplanes speeding across a sensitive median line dividing the Taiwan Strait.

It also cut off contact with the United States over a number of issues from military matters to combating climate change, in retaliation for what it viewed as a violation of its sovereignty.

This time, Beijing has already threatened to “resolutely fight back” if a Tsai-McCarthy meeting goes ahead.

It also slammed Washington for allowing Tsai to stopover in the US while en route to and from official visits in Central America, warning it could lead to “serious” confrontation between the two powers.

A defiant Tsai staked out her own ground, pledging as she took off on her 10-day trip not to let “external pressure” stop Taiwan from connecting with the world and like-minded democracies.

But the optics of the meeting, taking place in California and not Taiwan, and its timing – at a particularly thorny moment in China’s foreign relations and ahead of a presidential election in Taiwan that could reset the tone of its relationship with Beijing – may see Beijing tread more carefully this time, or at least not escalate further, analysts say.

“This puts the burden on China not to overreact, because any overreaction is only going to push China further away from the world,” stated Yun Sun, director of the China Program at the Stimson Center think tank in Washington.

That doesn’t mean, however, that Beijing won’t be closely watching Tsai’s movements as it calibrates its response – and decides how much military might to flex over her meeting with an American lawmaker on American soil.

The opacity of China’s system – and the potential for competing interests within its vast bureaucracy – also make it difficult to accurately predict its response.

According to recent reports, “Every time Taiwan does anything that China doesn’t like, the Chinese react with their own military coercion,” Sun said. But in the current situation, “they have to consider the consequences of overreaction,” she added.

The expected meeting, which McCarthy’s office revealed earlier this week would take place on Wednesday, also comes at a precarious moment in US-China relations.

Washington and Beijing are struggling to stabilize their communication amid flaring tensions over complications from a downed suspected Chinese surveillance balloon to semiconductor supply chains – raising the stakes of potential damage to that relationship if Beijing lashes out as it did when Tsai met Pelosi.

Industry observers note that taiwan is still feeling the fallout of that response last August, with Chinese military forces now regularly making incursions over what had previously been an informal but largely respected border of control between Beijing and Taipei in the Taiwan Strait. Taiwan’s official Central News Agency also reported Monday that Tsai would meet with McCarthy, citing Tsai’s presidential office.

But a meeting between Tsai and the leader of the Republican majority in the US House of Representatives, who ranks second in line to the Presidency, would mark another symbolic moment for Taiwan and the US, which only maintain unofficial ties.

It has been revealed that for Tsai, who is entering the final year of her two-term presidency, “it’s clearly a capstone event,” according to Wen-Ti Sung, a political scientist at the Australian National University’s Taiwan Studies Program. “She has this image as the Taiwanese president who has taken US-Taiwan relations to newly introduced heights, and who … has been able to give Taiwan almost unprecedented international visibility,” he stated.

That increased visibility – and enhanced cooperation with the US – has followed China’s mounting pressure on the island, which sits fewer than 110 miles (177 kilometers) from the mainland coast.

China’s Communist Party claims the self-governing island democracy as its own despite never having controlled it, and has vowed to take the island, by force if necessary.

In a recent development, china thinks it's diplomatically isolating Taiwan. It isn't.

The party has undertaken a sweeping expansion of its military capabilities over the past decade under leader Xi Jinping – and ramped up its pervasive economic, diplomatic and military pressure on Taiwan.

That’s driven concerns, among some in Washington, that Beijing is preparing for an invasion, though China’s official language still suggests that scenario is not its preferred option for achieving the claimed goal of “reunification.”.

It is those pressures – and how to support Taiwan against unilateral actions by Beijing – that are likely to be on the table when Tsai, McCarthy and a bipartisan group of US lawmakers sit down on Wednesday.

Congress has been a pillar of increasing American support for Taiwan in recent years. Lawmakers regularly visit the island and drive bipartisan legislation enhancing support and cooperation.

While the US switched its diplomatic relations to Beijing decades ago, it maintains unofficial ties with Taiwan and is bound by law to provide the democratic island with the means to defend itself.

Under Washington’s longstanding “One China” policy, the US acknowledges China’s position that Taiwan is part of China, but has never officially recognized Beijing’s claim to the island of 23 million.

Though McCarthy does not have Pelosi’s decades-long record of advocacy regarding China, the California Republican is now a leading voice pushing for closer scrutiny of Beijing, and meeting Tsai could help him to burnish that image.

Last month, McCarthy told reporters that meeting Tsai in the US would not impact whether he travels to Taiwan in the future – something he had earlier mentioned he wanted to do.

A meeting in California, on US soil, is widely seen as less likely to provoke Beijing than a McCarthy visit to Taiwan.

Pelosi’s trip – the first from a lawmaker of that rank to the island in 25 years – generated a fever pitch of nationalist and anti-US rhetoric in mainland China.

This time, so far, domestic conversation in China’s heavily controlled media sphere has been significantly muted.

But the stakes remain high – including for Beijing itself – over how it responds, analysts say.

As Taiwan prepares for a presidential election in January, a fierce response could push voters away from Taiwan’s main opposition party Kuomintang (KMT), widely seen as more friendly toward Beijing.

It could also jar with another high profile trip happening now: a tour of mainland China from former Taiwan president and senior KMT member Ma Ying-jeou, the first visit from a current or former Taiwan leader since the end of the Chinese Civil War in 1949.

Ma’s tour is a “once in a half a century opportunity to send a conciliatory message between the two sides, Beijing shouldn’t want to tank that,” remarked Sung, the political scientist.

What you need to know about China-Taiwan tensions.

China is also acutely aware that its actions toward Taiwan are under a significantly brighter global spotlight following the invasion of Ukraine by Russian President Vladimir Putin, a close diplomatic partner of Xi. Putin’s rhetoric over Ukraine has echoes of how Xi speaks of Taiwan.

Beijing has recently sought to position itself as an agent of peace in that conflict – especially as it aims to repair frayed ties with Europe.

This week, as Tsai is expected to meet with McCarthy, French President Emmanuel Macron and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen will head to China – an crucial opportunity that Xi may not want to overshadow with military posturing.

An aggressive response also risks stoking confrontation with the US, not yet six months after Xi and US President Joe Biden called to enhance communication during a face-to-face meeting in Bali.

“(A less overtly aggressive response) would imply that Beijing does not wish to escalate tension with the US to a level that can risk getting out of hand,” said Steve Tsang, director of the SOAS China Institute in London.

“A reset in US-China ties is not on the agenda, but an easing of tension is not beyond the realm of possibility.”.

CNN’s Wayne Chang contributed reporting.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Watch: Miliband spoke to the BBC following the summit in Brussels.

A deal agreed between the UK and the European Union on Friday will come into force regardless of whether the two sides can negotiate a separate tuition fees agreement, Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband has told the BBC.

The measures agreed in Brussels include scrapping most checks on British food exports in return for the UK following some EU regulations from 2028, and a latest youth mobility scheme.

However, a proposal from the bloc to lower the level of tuition fees paid by EU students in the UK has not been agreed.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said she was "confident" a solution would be found, with Prime Minister Andy Burnham adding "me too" during a press conference announcing the deal.

Meanwhile, asked in his interview with the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg programme whether rejoining the EU would be looked at, Miliband noted "all the options will be on the table".

It came after the prime minister mentioned that he would discuss possible ideas for even closer ties with the bloc in the coming months.

What is the EU-UK youth experience scheme and when will it start?

Burnham gets his first taste of EU dealmaking and seems hungry for more.

Faisal Islam: This cost-cutting UK-EU deal doesn't mean lower prices will follow.

UK and EU leaders have hailed the closer cooperation agreement, with Burnham calling the deal a "win-win" that could lower the cost of living and reduce red tape.

The prime minister said the Treasury believes the deal could boost the UK economy by up to Â£17bn a year.

EU sources had earlier suggested that the bloc might hold up applying the wider deal until it was agreed that EU students who wanted to study in the UK would pay the same fees as British students.

Miliband remarked it was "absolutely clear" the agreements on food exports, energy and youth mobility would apply, even though there has not been a deal on tuition fees.

"President von der Leyen... was very clear about this at the press conference we just had. She stated there are those three agreements and then there's a separate piece of paper and a separate glitch, which is looking at the issue of tuition," he said.

Asked again whether the agreements would definitely become law, the foreign secretary stated: "Yes, absolutely.".

"The dates are set out in 2028 when these things are coming in, we're introducing legislation in Parliament, so definitely.".

Miliband noted there would be "no cost" to the UK taxpayer for anything agreed at Friday's summit, adding that there would be no fresh contributions to the EU budget.

He stated previously announced agreements on EU schemes like Erasmus+ were a "separate decision" and the summit "was not about cost to the taxpayer".

Speaking on Friday, Burnham argued that polling suggests the UK public "want closer ties" with the EU and the deal "delivers that".

Miliband told the BBC that "of course all the options will be on the table" when pressed on whether rejoining the bloc would be considered, adding that "we will look at the benefits and the costs of all the different options".

He stated that while he accepted the result of the 2016 Brexit referendum, "the world has changed massively".

"Europe is changing too, so we've got to look at what that means. It's not about this parliament, we're respecting the red lines in this parliament," he added.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said the deal was "not fair", arguing that UK farmers would have to follow rules set in Brussels and young people from the EU would "compete" with young Britons struggling to get jobs at home.

She also claimed Burnham had "plucked" the Â£17bn figure out of thin air, and remarked the only modelling she had seen of how the agreement could boost the economy put the figure at "0.0%".

Reform UK leader Nigel Farage stated Friday marked a "betrayal of the British people" and a good day for the EU to "try and humiliate" the UK.

Farage, who was a leading figure in the 2016 campaign to get Britain out of the EU, wrote on social media: "Like every prime minister before him, Burnham is a total fraud.".

Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey said there needed to be more than "tweaks" to the UK's relationship to the EU.

"A youth mobility scheme is a massive step forward, but it's nowhere near enough. We need a whole upcoming deal that actually works for Britain, and fast.".

Speaking to BBC Radio 4's Today programme, the University of Manchester's vice chancellor Professor Duncan Ivison said closer UK-EU relations were a "good thing" but "the glitch of tuition fees is something we do have to figure out because there is a cost".

He warned that EU students being allowed to pay domestic university fees would "take Â£500m, we estimate, out of the higher education sector at a time where there's a lot of pressure on the sector".

He added: "If EU students come and are paying domestic fees, it's not clear we'd be able to increase the number of places for EU students anyway.".

Environment Secretary Dame Angela Eagle stated the Treasury and Department for Education would work with universities to find a solution during negotiations.

It has been revealed that she told BBC Breakfast: "I don't think anybody wants to do deals that negatively impact anything. We want win-win deals.".

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The simple answer is yes, an iPhone can tolerate a 140-watt charger, but it's not a simple process, and there are safety considerations.
  • Potential safety problems are generally on the charger's end.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The simple answer is yes, an iPhone can tolerate a 140-watt charger, but it's not a simple process, and there are safety considerations. A 140-watt charger is an upper limit that your iPhone will never reach because even the latest iPhone 18 Pro hits its cap at 52W. An iPhone can only pull what it can pull, and it's nowhere near 140W. USB PD used to top out at 100W, but the newer range is between 100W and 240W, now known as Extended Power Range (EPR). EPR adds 28V, 36V and 48V options. Once a device is in EPR mode, it has to send a "keep-alive" message every half second. If the charger doesn't receive that message, it drops back down to 5V. An iPhone's requirements are well below that threshold.

Potential safety problems are generally on the charger's end. Apple is pretty blunt about using third-party chargers that fail to meet safety standards, claiming it could cause injury and even death. Obviously, that's something iPhone consumers should avoid, so stick with reputable brands. Yes, Apple's own power adapters and cables are priced like they have 24k gold in them, but there are plenty of options out there that meet safety standards and cost much less.

Sources indicate that far less than 140W. The iPhone 17, 17 Pro and 17 Pro Max reach 50 percent in about 20 minutes with a 40W or higher adapter. The iPhone Air and iPhone 17e only need 20W to hit 50 percent in roughly half an hour. For an iPhone 15 or 16 (or an older Lightning model like the iPhone 14 with a USB-C to Lightning cable), a USB PD adapter 18W or greater is needed for fast charging. The iPhone 18 Pro series and the iPhone Duo step things up a bit. The best and fastest charger for these phones is a 60W adapter with Adjustable Voltage Supply (AVS) and USB PD 3.2, plus a USB-C cable that can handle 60W or more.

It has been revealed that none of that approaches 140W. The best use case for 140W+ is a high-performance laptop or charging several devices at the same time. If you have an Apple adapter (Apple doesn't supply them with iPhones/iPads for environmental purposes), the wattage is printed on the top or bottom. Apple prints the Dynamic Power Symbol on their 40W chargers. You can also get a fairly accurate estimate of charging time directly from your iPhone. On iOS 18 or later, a Slow Charger message appears on the Lock Screen and under Settings > Battery. iOS 26 ramps up the convenience by alerting you when you're using an incompatible charger that isn't charging your iPhone.

According to recent reports, not much, unless it's a USB-C port with Power Delivery. At base specs, USB 2.0 ports supply 5V at 500mA or 2.5W. USB 3.0 and 3.1 ports bump it up to 900mA or 4.5W. The Battery Charging 1.2 spec ports can reach 1.5A or 7.5W. If you prefer to charge from a PC or laptop, it's a bit chaotic. For instance, orange ports on Intel NUC PCs are rated at 1.5A, and the blue ones are 900 milliamps. Black ports are typically USB 2.0 and have a modest 2.5W default. Those examples sound pretty sluggish because they are. Plug an iPhone 18 Pro Max into a USB 2.0, and it's gonna be a while. The iPhone 15 and later are capped at 7.5W on a USB-A charger. Fortunately, USB-C is a major upgrade over USB-A, with 15W (5V at 3A) without Power Delivery.

Recent findings suggest that with Power Delivery, it skyrockets to 100W in the Standard Power Range and 240W with EPR. On top of that, standard USB-C cables are rated for 3A, hitting their ceiling at 60W, while 100W feature e-marked 5A cables. These cables have a tiny chip that tells the charger what it can handle. EPR cables encompass everything above 100W. A "typical USB port" is ultimately defined by the individual. For someone who uses a fairly standard 20W adapter for an iPhone, a USB-A port may be considered typical, but a specialized USB-A charger can push up to 18W. In other words, what is "typical" depends on what you're using and what you're used to.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Economists flag rising recession risk as government forecasts economy will grow by less than 2% in 2027 and 2028.

Follow our Australia politics live blog for latest updates.

Get our daily political email, free app or daily news podcast.

Jim Chalmers has warned Australians that “things will get a bit harder before they get easier”, revealing next month’s budget patch will show unemployment climbing above 5% alongside slower economic growth for the next two years.

As economists flagged rising recessionary risks, the treasurer used a ministerial statement during question time to reveal what he described as “concerning” economic numbers in the upcoming mid-year economic and fiscal outlook.

Alongside higher unemployment, high fuel costs meant inflation would slow from 4.7% now to only “the mid-3s” by the middle of next year – or about 1 percentage point higher than anticipated in the May budget.

The economy was now expected to grow by less than 2% in both 2027 and 2028.

“We say with humility and with honesty that things might get a bit harder before they get easier,” Chalmers told parliament.

According to recent reports, “If Treasury was updating the mid-year forecasts today, they would reflect this difficult environment we’re in. In the near term, they’d forecast softer growth, higher inflation and higher unemployment.”.

With a majority of Australians blaming public spending for driving this year’s inflation outbreak, Chalmers promised that the mid-year economic and fiscal outlook will include “net savings” to assist in the ongoing battle against persistently high price pressures.

“It’s not a mini-budget full of fresh initiatives but it will have some budget-sized savings. At this stage, we expect to more than offset our new spending decisions, without slashing and burning the services people rely on,” he noted.

News last week that the unemployment rate had climbed to 4.9% in October has turbocharged fears that a series of Reserve Bank interest rate hikes are weighing more heavily than anticipated – and that the economy could even tip into a deeper downturn next year.

Chalmers mentioned the government’s short-term goal was “cutting spending enough, without threatening growth” – an approach he described as “a delicate balance”.

“We know that no realistic amount of savings makes inflation go away, but too much latest spending can make it worse,” he said.

With the full effect of the five rate hikes only likely to become apparent through 2027, Shane Oliver, AMP’s chief economist, predicted economic growth would slump from 2.3%, to below 1%.

“We could flirt with recession next year,” Oliver said, putting the chances of a more severe downturn at a “high and rising” 40%.

Official figures on Wednesday are likely to show inflation climbing to nearly 5%, and Oliver agreed with the treasurer that getting the settings right in the mid-year budget would be “a difficult balancing act”.

“The government has been copping political blame for inflation, and Chalmers is under a lot of pressure to cut [spending]; but if he cuts too much it could accentuate the recession risks.”.

The treasurer foreshadowed that any new spending decisions – such as Monday’s announcement that the $25 price cap on prescription medicine would be extended until the end of the decade at a cost of $242m – would be more than offset by savings measures.

But he also flagged that the mix of a weaker economy and “massive unavoidable spending commitments” meant bigger deficits in the later years of the forward estimates period.

“It would not be responsible to fully offset these substantial changes to revenue and payments that flow through automatically from weaker economic parameters,” he argued.
