#70161. Should you go with a headphone DAC/amp combo or a stack?

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (620 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Engadget ↗ Open Full Page

Should you go with a headphone DAC/amp combo or a stack?

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (620 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Both will do a fine job, and it depends on what you need from your gear.
  • You don't always need a DAC and amp to enjoy music through headphones.
  • A DAC and a headphone amp can come together in a single unit (usually known as a DAC/amp) or as a stack of separate units.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Both will do a fine job, and it depends on what you need from your gear.

You don't always need a DAC and amp to enjoy music through headphones. If your computer or laptop's headphone jack already delivers clean audio at a comfortable volume, then you're probably fine. Some MacBooks from 2021 and later, for example, support both low- and high-impedance headphones and can deliver up to 3 volts RMS through their headphone jacks when you use headphones rated between 150 and 1,000 ohms. If your headphone jack isn't quite as capable, or if you're not satisfied with the sound, though, then it's time to spend on some hardware.

A DAC and a headphone amp can come together in a single unit (usually known as a DAC/amp) or as a stack of separate units. And while the latter seems like the more serious setup, it doesn't necessarily mean you'll enjoy a better listening experience. The main job of a DAC is to turn digital audio signals into analog signals, while the amplifier takes those analog signals and makes them loud enough to power your headphones. Both a DAC/amp combo and a stack do the same thing, and which you go for largely depends on your headphones, how much flexibility you need and, of course, your budget.

For most listeners, a DAC/amp is the way to go, especially if you're trying to improve your computer's audio without taking up too much space. Not only is a single unit more convenient, but it also means fewer cables dangling around and one less power adapter to worry about. You can even use a portable USB-C DAC/amp dongle designed for smartphones, but desktop versions usually offer better connectivity and power.

DAC/amps can also offer better value than separates, too. Schiit's Magni 6 sells for $169 with its optional internal USB DAC. Conversely, you can buy the Magni 6 sans DAC for $99 and pair it with the Modi 5 DAC for $149 (or $164 with a power adapter). That brings the total to over $250, and you don't even get an interconnect cable. The Modi 5 has optical and coaxial inputs, sure, but that doesn't automatically equate to better sound.

DAC/amp combos don't necessarily have to come with major compromises, either. The $549 JDS Labs Element IV delivers up to 3.2 watts per channel into 32 ohms, and comes with features like automatic gain switching, EQ and even preamp outputs for powered speakers. That's more than enough for many demanding headphones, eliminating the need for a dedicated amplifier. The downside, of course, is that you're stuck with the combo and can't upgrade piecemeal.

While DAC/amp combos are great, a stack can still make sense for audiophiles who use a wide variety of headphones or who like to tinker with their hi-fi setup. Going with separates gives you the freedom to upgrade the amplifier down the line without giving up a perfectly capable DAC, or vice versa.

Recent findings suggest that certain headphones may also benefit from the power a dedicated amp can provide. Some high-impedance headphones just ask for a lot of power, while planar magnetic models, for example, can combine low impedance and low sensitivity. Let's take the HiFiMAN Susvara Unveiled, for example, which has a 45-ohm impedance and only 86 dB sensitivity. The Absolute Sound advises at least 6 watts of amplification, so a standalone amp may be the better choice here. However, too much power can be a bad thing, too: a very powerful amp may result in audible hiss with very sensitive headphones. So start by checking your headphones' power requirements and the amplifier's noise performance instead of just assuming that you need a beefy amp.

US Army to detonate tonnes of unstable explosives in Iowa despite court order

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (578 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The US Army prepares to move ahead with detonating five tonnes of degraded explosives in Iowa despite a ruling to halt it indefinitely, a new court filing shows.
  • "To protect its personnel and the surrounding communities, the Army needs to take swift action," the justice department notified the court on Saturday.
  • The court had ordered a pause after environmental groups sued to stop the detonation, arguing the army failed to consider safer alternatives.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The US Army prepares to move ahead with detonating five tonnes of degraded explosives in Iowa despite a ruling to halt it indefinitely, a new court filing shows.

"To protect its personnel and the surrounding communities, the Army needs to take swift action," the justice department notified the court on Saturday. "Protection of human health and the environment demand action now, not delay.".

The court had ordered a pause after environmental groups sued to stop the detonation, arguing the army failed to consider safer alternatives.

Recent findings suggest that the detonation was originally scheduled for Friday at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown. The army now looks to act by 24 November under an emergency exemption.

In the newly introduced filing, the Department of the Army argued that a controlled detonation was necessary to protect the public from an unplanned explosion, a risk it remarked would become more likely as temperatures were set to fall in the coming days.

"There is an immediate risk that the lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant will explode as temperatures are expected to drop below 30 degrees Fahrenheit (-1C) in the next several days," the filing states.

It argued that the army had removed the doors to the bunker where the barrels were stored in preparation for the detonation and that made the explosives more "vulnerable to temperature changes".

The government has not released details for the rescheduled detonation.

Earlier, the army had warned residents to leave their homes for six hours on the original scheduled day of the explosion, for the duration of the explosion and until the dust settled. An advisory warned "all humans" to avoid being outside in the affected areas while the demolition detonation was set to take place.

It has been revealed that lead azide is a highly volatile compound used as a detonator. Earlier this year, the IAAAP found that the material had degraded over time to the point where it was now too risky to move the material, according to Iowa Public Radio.

On Friday, the military mentioned it was working with the Department of Health and Human Services and the EPA to ensure the explosion was done in the safest manner possible.

Military and environmental officials determined that detonating it in place was the safest way to eliminate the explosive safety hazard.

The EPA, which granted an emergency permit to detonate 68 drums of the material, said it did so because the explosion risk "presented an imminent and substantial threat to human health and the environment".

One of the Environmental groups suing to pause the detonation, the Iowa Environmental Council, argued that many Iowans living within the risk-zone were unaware that the explosion was scheduled to happen.

"There is no safe level of lead exposure, and Iowans were given just days to prepare for the November 20 detonation," the organisation said in a press statement.

The Iowa Environmental Council and Sierra Club, which filed the lawsuit on Thursday that prompted the court-ordered pause, filed a fresh motion on Sunday in response to the army's filing.

The group asks the court to pause proceedings so that it may submit additional information before the scheduled detonation.

The motion includes declarations from environmental experts and local officials who support pausing the detonation, citing a lack of public notice and questioning the Army's claim that delay would cause significant risks.

US army warns detonation of unstable explosives will create toxic plume.

Breaking: China commits to low-carbon electrification and help for others to improve

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (918 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theguardian

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Exclusive: Countries at Cop31 are being urged to commit to deriving 35% of their energy from electricity by 2035.
  • China is pushing for rapid electrification of its economy using low-carbon energy and will help other countries do the same, a senior member of the Chinese delegation at the Cop31 UN climate summit has mentioned.
  • In a recent development, wang Yi, a professor of energy and environment policy at the Chinese Academy of Sciences and a senior adviser to China’s government, said: “End-use electrification is a very clear direction.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Exclusive: Countries at Cop31 are being urged to commit to deriving 35% of their energy from electricity by 2035.

China is pushing for rapid electrification of its economy using low-carbon energy and will help other countries do the same, a senior member of the Chinese delegation at the Cop31 UN climate summit has mentioned.

In a recent development, wang Yi, a professor of energy and environment policy at the Chinese Academy of Sciences and a senior adviser to China’s government, said: “End-use electrification is a very clear direction. We can follow this direction while making the source of electricity clean. That’s the way to go forward.”.

China is the biggest emitter of greenhouse gases by far, producing more than a quarter of the world’s total, so its push for electrification is significant.

But in the second draft text of the probable outcome from Cop31, released on Thursday, the electrification pledge was downgraded to one of a suite of voluntary options countries can take up to reduce their greenhouse gas emissions.

In an interview with the Guardian at the talks, Wang mentioned: “China will do our best to realise clean end-use electrification, and also help other countries to improve. China has significantly reduced the cost of clean technology and products and we would like to share our experience with other countries.”.

Experts have remarked electrification is the next vital step in the shift to a low-carbon economy, as the only way to diminish the close to 80% of fossil fuels still used for primary energy, mostly for transport, heating and industry.

While civil society organisations want any commitment made on electrification to specify that it must be met from clean sources, a pledge that leaves the choice to countries is likely to have more widespread support, as many – including China and India – are resistant to anything they feel smacks of “top down” interference in national intends.

But campaigners argue that allowing individual countries to decide risks leaving the door open to more gas-fired power plants. Some compromise language is also possible that would urge countries to decarbonise their power.

Last year, electricity made up nearly 30% of China’s energy use and it is on track to make that 35% by 2030. Electricity is several times more efficient than fossil fuels, meaning that it takes far less energy to run electric vehicles, heat pumps and industrial processes than their fossil fuel counterparts.

Wang noted China was happy with the 2035 target, but that it would be harder to meet if the electricity was required to come entirely from low-carbon sources. “For this target, no problem. But if you think about ensuring clean electrification, that may be a little bit difficult, even for China. For other countries, it’s even more difficult,” he said.

Industry observers note that china still has a large number of coal-fired power stations and is planning some latest ones, though fewer than before. Wang said this would be used for back-up during the transition to clean energy.

Recent findings suggest that one of the key problems at Cop31 is the “transition away from fossil fuels”, which was one of the resolutions passed at the Cop28 summit in Dubai in 2023, but which countries have failed to flesh out since. The phrase was included in the first draft of the “cover decision” outcome from Cop31, presented on Monday, but excised from the second draftissued on Thursday, to the dismay of many countries and campaigners.

Wang said: “We agree with paragraph 28 of the UAE consensus [the transition resolution]. But maybe different countries have different roadmaps. It’s very difficult to have only one unified roadmap for every country. So maybe we will help other countries to have their own country-based solutions, to realise their own national way of establishing a upcoming renewable-based power system.”.

China is also concerned about trade barriers to its clean technology exports, including the tariffs that the US under Donald Trump has placed on Chinese goods, and the “carbon border adjustment mechanism” (CBAM) imposed by the EU. The CBAM penalises imports from countries with looser regulations on carbon than the EU, which forces companies in high-carbon sectors to pay for their carbon emissions in order to level the playing field.

Some smaller developing countries have criticised the EU for its CBAM, warning that it will hamper their manufacturing industries. The EU said it had processes in place to ensure smaller developing countries were not hurt.

Wang called for more work on trade concerns at Cops. “They must come together to find a unified approach,” he stated. “China and other developing countries, including the global south, disagree [with the EU] on this. But that’s why we should continue to strengthen our dialogue.”.

According to recent reports, jiangwen Guo, a senior research fellow at the Chatham House thinktank, stated other countries could learn from China. “China has very consistent top-down policies [and] sets a clear direction with high consistency, then follows with learning by doing,” she said. “In the great energy transition, there is no one ahead of China. China is creating the model for the globe.”.

Recent findings suggest that negotiators at Cop31, which was scheduled to end at 6pm on Friday, were sent home late on Friday after the talks stalled, with a upcoming draft text of a “cover decision” marking the main outcome of the negotiations not thought likely to emerge until some time on Saturday morning. The talks are likely to continue into Saturday and potentially beyond.

This free 'Swiss Army Knife' for macOS can replace your utility apps

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Vorssaint is a powerful, modular utility suite, provided permissions are carefully managed.
  • macOS offers one of the most refined desktop experiences, but owners looking for more granular control of their desktops might find the OS' native options limiting.
  • It has been revealed that vorssaint is a third-party, open source application that aims to resolve macOS' productivity and customization pain points with a single menu-bar application.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Vorssaint is a powerful, modular utility suite, provided permissions are carefully managed.

macOS offers one of the most refined desktop experiences, but owners looking for more granular control of their desktops might find the OS' native options limiting. Unlike Microsoft's PowerToys, which includes a collection of over 25 productivity and customization tools, Mac users must often turn to a fragmented selection of third-party applications to achieve similar levels of control. For example, macOS' native window tiling is serviceable at best, allowing for only a few tiling options regardless of screen size. Similarly, the OS doesn't natively support independent volume control and output device selection for individual applications. This is where Vorssaint, the Swiss Army Knife of macOS utility apps, comes into the picture.

It has been revealed that vorssaint is a third-party, open source application that aims to resolve macOS' productivity and customization pain points with a single menu-bar application. The app groups together a range of utility tools and nifty quick toggles to streamline productivity. The project is hosted on GitHub, and has earned over 33,000 stars and 230 contributors.

In a recent development, vorssaint includes an impressive collection of utilities that aims to improve how users interact with their Macs. Its window-tiling feature offers more control over how users arrange their application windows, including edge snapping and shortcuts. The app also includes a toggle for clamshell mode, enabling MacBooks to continue running even with their lids closed, while its "Keep Awake" feature allows users to control when or if their Macs can enter a sleep state.

The application suite also includes several handy tools that streamline daily workflows. For example, its screenshot utility supports scrolling screenshots, which makes it possible to capture content that extends beyond what's visible on the screen. People can also edit captured screenshots with the app's in-built image editing tool. Similarly, Vorssaint's media tool is capable of video compression, image conversion and text extraction from images. Meanwhile, its system monitoring tool extends beyond Mac's Activity Monitor, providing valuable information on thermals, memory usage and network speed.

According to recent reports, these are just a few examples of what Vorssaint offers. The suite also includes a graphical interface for Homebrew, URL cleaner and a powerful command bar. The command bar is akin to Apple's Spotlight search, but a lot more exciting. Its functionality extends beyond just searching apps and files; it can also be used to perform quick mathematical calculations, unit conversions and access most of Vorssaint's utilities by simply searching for them.

Vorssaint's robust utility stack undoubtedly makes it a promising productivity suite for power people. However, some of its powerful tools require sensitive macOS permissions. Depending on what features users install, the app may request permissions for Accessibility, Screen Recording, Full Disk Access and Automation. While granting these permissions is necessary to allow Vorssaint to perform some of its functions like taking screenshots, uninstalling applications and other system-level operations, users must understand what it means to grant system-level permissions to applications, especially those built by third-party developers.

This is where Vorssaint's modular design becomes particularly useful, allowing users to choose specific modules according to their requirements. For example, someone particularly interested in streamlining window management can choose to install only the Window layout module, and need not grant it screen recording and app management permissions. This selective approach lets users retain the modules they without having to risk granting sensitive permissions.

AI claimed a solution to the 167-year-old Riemann hypothesis — and a human did, too

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, it’s a big week for Levent Alpöge: The mathematician saw his employer, Anthropic, become the first publicly traded frontier AI lab.
  • “The precise timing is horrible,” he wrote in an essay announcing his findings and describing how he messaged Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei last Sunday night to ask how to announce that he had found a Lean-compilable solution to the Riemann hypothesis, which dates back to 1859 and is among the Millennium Prize math problems.
  • Industry observers note that the hypothesis conjectures that there is a hidden structure underlying the appearance of prime numbers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, it’s a big week for Levent Alpöge: The mathematician saw his employer, Anthropic, become the first publicly traded frontier AI lab. He also appears to have solved one of the most key problems in mathematics.

“The precise timing is horrible,” he wrote in an essay announcing his findings and describing how he messaged Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei last Sunday night to ask how to announce that he had found a Lean-compilable solution to the Riemann hypothesis, which dates back to 1859 and is among the Millennium Prize math problems.

Industry observers note that the hypothesis conjectures that there is a hidden structure underlying the appearance of prime numbers. If the claimed result holds true, we’re entering sublime-mysteries-of-the-universe territory.

In a recent development, maybe the best way to understand how exciting this is to the mathematics community is to watch the experts puzzling through the result in a chat on Zulip. Mathematicians like Chris Birkbeck, a number theorist at the University of East Anglia, are posting thoughts like this ….

The cohomology bound is proved by what looks like an automorphy-lifting argument. It genuinely uses the existence of Galois representations attached to regular algebraic, polarized cuspidal automorphic representations of GL_n over CM fields, along with base change, Jacquet–Shalika, Clozel’s purity, Bernstein–Zelevinsky, the main theorem of CM, Deligne–Ribet and more.

For my part, I tapped out of mathematics at college calculus, so I can’t help decode exactly what that means.

But that comment was followed by 20 readers reacting 🤯.

In a recent development, it will be a while before the mathematics community feels like it has a handle on the proof, but most appear confident that the formalized Lean result will hold. Lean is an an open-source coding language used to express mathematical ideas as code, allowing proofs to be formally verified. Several participants in the Zulip chat, including MIT mathematician Andrew Sutherland, say they have successfully confirmed that Alpöge’s solution can be compiled successfully.

Alpöge appeared in his essay to feel a bit guilty about releasing the proof without a truly human-intelligible explanation, but his obsession with the problem since childhood made him feel he “could not live” if he waited to release the finding.

Alpöge described a “stream-of-consciousness jaunt through the experience of finding all the pieces of the argument through incredible confusion with Claude” with more than a hint of AI euphoria, describing how the model “flew, and danced, and sparkled near that finish line.”.

However, for all that action to mean anything, we’ll have to wait for humans to be able to understand the result and explain it to each other, something Alpöge has committed to pursue.

Alpöge and a collaborator, NYU mathematician Tristan Buckmaster, also released another key proof related to the Navier-Stokes equations, problems that helped kick off the race between frontier labs and mathematicians to solve outstanding problems this summer.

Recent findings suggest that meanwhile, Ravi Vakil, a Stanford professor and the president of the American Mathematics Association, posted a proof of the General Riemann hypothesis written by Stanford postdoc Alessandro Masullo, noting that “it is all human, with no AI. The hope was to bring Alessandro to Stanford for a year to polish the writing and then announce it after running it by enough people. Now it seems best to put out the current draft.”.

Without being expressed in Lean, it is too early to say whether the proof checks out, much less if anyone understands it.

Recent findings suggest that in a brief introduction to his proof, which he mentioned is the result of 12 years of work, Masullo wrote that “if any message at all this work is meant to send to the mathematician who feels discouraged by the pace and tone of the current climate, it is this: we are still here. We are very much alive. We are not going anywhere.”.

This story has been updated to include that Alpöge’s Lean proof has been checked by independent sources.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The Democratic Party has won the largest majority in the US House of Representatives since 1992, after Democrat Chuck Hubbard unseated Republican Representative Virginia Foxx in North Carolina.
  • Recent findings suggest that the race was called on Sunday, with Hubbard beating Foxx by 330 votes with 99% counted.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Watch: Democrat who unseated 21-year Republican incumbent notes party needs to 'bring change'.

The Democratic Party has won the largest majority in the US House of Representatives since 1992, after Democrat Chuck Hubbard unseated Republican Representative Virginia Foxx in North Carolina.

Recent findings suggest that the race was called on Sunday, with Hubbard beating Foxx by 330 votes with 99% counted. It was one of the closest contests of the recent midterm elections, in which Democrats also secured the Senate.

The party has now won at least 258 House seats in the midterms compared to Republicans, who hold at least 173 seats, with four races still yet to be called.

Neither party had won as many House races since 1992, when Bill Clinton won the presidency and Democrats won a total of 258 seats.

View the 2026 midterm election results.

It has been revealed that sunday's result came after Foxx, who has represented North Carolina's 5th Congressional District since 2005, requested a recount. This is allowed under state law when the margin of victory is under 1%.

In a recent development, "I think the American people are just sick of what's going on and they wanted a change. They voted for change," Hubbard told the BBC News Channel after his victory. He pledged to work alongside his fellow lawmakers to hold President Donald Trump accountable.

Earlier, he wrote on X that he had spoken to Foxx, "who graciously conceded following the results of the recount process".

Hubbard added: "I deeply appreciate her commitment to a smooth transition of the office and constituent casework. We may not always agree, but we both love North Carolina and the people of the Fifth District.".

Foxx, meanwhile, mentioned in a statement: "After running a campaign focused on my track record of commonsense solutions and conservative values, I'm humbled and grateful that so many North Carolina voters responded by supporting my candidacy, even if we came up just a few votes short.".

Virginia Foxx spent a decade in the North Carolina Senate before representing the state in the House of Representatives.

Hubbard's win, which comes after he lost to Foxx in the 2024 midterms by nine percentage points, followed a number of Democratic victories in deeply Republican districts including South Carolina, Texas, Alaska and Iowa.

Hubbard, like many Democrats running in the midterms, focused on the rising cost of living in the US during the war with Iran - a top glitch for voters.

Trump himself - as well as Vice President JD Vance - have suggested inflation caused by the war in Iran was probably to blame for the Republican losses.

Hubbard has also remarked he will also prioritise working families and small businesses, supporting public education and expanding access to affordable healthcare, according to his website.

The remaining House races yet to be called are in Tennessee and Minnesota, while two elections in Louisiana will go to a runoff in December.   • The country has been gripped by fears of AI-assisted exam cheating since last Sunday, when the top scorer in a national tax accountancy exam confessed to using a miniature camera and smartphone to achieve a near-perfect score, just four days before the crucial university entrance exam, known as the suneung.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Choi Kyo-jin says he ‘failed to prepare adequately’ for entrance exams following last-minute scramble to tighten measures.

South Korea’s education minister has resigned after an AI-assisted cheating scandal that erupted in the lead-up to key university entrance exams last week.

The country has been gripped by fears of AI-assisted exam cheating since last Sunday, when the top scorer in a national tax accountancy exam confessed to using a miniature camera and smartphone to achieve a near-perfect score, just four days before the crucial university entrance exam, known as the suneung.

The cheat’s confession sent officials scrambling to roll out a slew of preventive measures for the university entrance exams, including blocking public wifi in testing areas.

The unprecedented crackdown included doubling the number of supervisors and sending emergency alerts to detect any smartphones illegally smuggled into the exam centres.

Recent findings suggest that students were also told to turn up with pencils only. Erasers were provided by the test centres, as authorities tried to reduce the chances of concealed digital devices disguised as stationery.

In addition, exam-takers were asked to avoid wearing clothes with buttons. Those who failed to comply were told they would have stickers placed over the buttons to prevent the use of hidden cameras.

The government promised a reward of at least $75,000 (£57,300) for anyone reporting cheating or misconduct, with reduced penalties for those who turned in their accomplices.

But the education minister, Choi Kyo-jin, struggled to reassure the public, and teachers’ unions criticised the government response as belated.

In a recent development, “The exam concluded without any major incidents … However, as the minister in charge, I do not believe I am immune from public criticism that we failed to prepare adequately in advance,” Choi wrote on X. “Now that the exam is over, I take full responsibility and hereby offer my resignation.”.

The president, Lee Jae Myung, accepted his resignation, the presidential office remarked.

It has been revealed that the annual, eight-hour suneung determines which university a candidate can attend and, in turn, their future prospects. It is widely seen as a ticket to prestigious universities, well-paid jobs and even better marriage prospects in the highly competitive country.

Asked during a parliamentary hearing on Monday whether he was confident that authorities could catch would-be cheaters on exam day, Choi, 72, replied: “Due to my age, I am not confident I could.” His response rapidly drew a public backlash.

Choi did not appear at press conferences in the days leading up to Thursday’s exam, and a vice-minister instead confirmed the preventive measures.

The person who cheated in the national tax accountancy exam mentioned in a video posted to his lawyer’s YouTube account that he had photographed the questions with a concealed microcamera, sent them to an AI system and read the answers from a smartphone. “I cheated in the tax accountant exam,” he said. “My top placing is not the result of legitimate effort.”.

The scandal has rattled a ‌country where standardised tests largely dictate social mobility and career trajectories.

Sources indicate that south Korea goes to great lengths to ensure the smooth running of the suneung. Aircraft takeoffs and landings are rescheduled during the 25-minute English listening paper to minimise noise, while artillery fire and tank movements are suspended. The stock market opens an hour late and cars are stopped 200 metres from every centre.

In the aftermath of the cheating scandal, the government announced that smart devices would have to be turned off and handed in for the suneung, while bags left in corridors would be checked for any devices that were still on. Exam officials also inspected all candidates’ glasses and watches, as well as their collars and sleeves for concealed cameras.

The government also sent emergency alerts to every phone in the country, which sounded at full volume and could not be silenced, in the hope of catching out anyone who had not handed in their device.

Officials stated 111 cases of misconduct involving electronic devices were identified during Thursday’s exam, nearly half of which were detected through the emergency alerts.

Industry observers note that A high-school student had filed a constitutional petition challenging the government’s decision to go ahead with the exam as planned. But a court rejected the request, citing insufficient evidence of irreparable harm.

Under the tightened measures, students caught cheating can be barred from retaking the exam for 10 years and face criminal prosecution.

With Agence France-Presse and Reuters.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The representative in the US House expected to chair the House Intelligence Committee in January, Jim Himes (D-Conn.), has threatened to withhold support for funding government-owned systems from SpaceX amid the ongoing inquiry into the use of Starshield in Ukraine.

According to recent reports, “SpaceX’s potentially unilateral modification of a U.S. Government contract, combined with its lack of responsiveness to congressional oversight, calls into question every contract the U.S. Government has with SpaceX,” Himes wrote in a letter to SpaceX founder Elon Musk on Friday.

CNN first reported the letter’s existence. The network also reported that Himes sent a classified communication to Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton with a similar message that it would be difficult for Congress to authorize funding for systems with SpaceX as the primary vendor.

Sources indicate that spaceX has developed the consumer Starlink service over the last decade, which provides high-speed Internet from low-Earth orbit to user terminals on Earth. For government customers, SpaceX has also developed Starshield, a suite of satellite services that includes a militarized version of Starlink communications. The US government has purchased Starshield services and extended access to Ukraine, although the terms governing that access are largely classified.

During the last several weeks, a controversy has erupted over interruptions to Starshield service in parts of Ukraine, cutting off connectivity to drones used to defend against Russian attacks.

Industry observers note that on October 19, for example, Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy remarked of Starshield on social media, “Unfortunately, we have established that the equipment stops functioning at speeds of 130–161 kilometers per hour in various sectors of the front. This is slowing down our frontline logistics and limiting the use of various types of drones, particularly mid-strike drones and interceptors of jet-powered ‘shaheds.’” Additional disruptions were reported a week ago.

The central question is who decided to curtail the performance of Starshield assets in Ukraine. Accounts have variously implicated Musk, SpaceX, the Pentagon, and the White House. Musk has noted that US officials control Starshield access, while defending SpaceX’s right to restrict the use of commercial Starlink service in war.

Recent findings suggest that “My ask to you is straightforward,” Himes wrote to Musk. “Explain the changes that were made to the Starshield service in October 2026, why those changes were made, and whether those changes were made unilaterally by SpaceX or were directed by a U.S. Government official.”.

The communications from Himes suggest that Congressional Democrats, who will control the House and Senate in January following decisive victories in the Midterm elections, are prepared to not just investigate the disruption of these SpaceX services in Ukraine, but to take action that could threaten SpaceX’s broader national security business.

“It is difficult for me to continue supporting the authorization of funding for these SpaceX-developed, government-owned systems, until I receive satisfactory answers to my questions about the Starshield service in Ukraine,” Himes wrote in his letter to Musk.

Various options are open to Congressional Democrats, as well as some Republicans who have raised similar concerns, including demanding classified briefings and documents and restricting funding through appropriations to the US Department of Defense and other federal departments. Notably, the US Space Force awarded SpaceX a $2.29 billion contract earlier this year to develop the Space Data Network Backbone intended to support the Golden Dome missile defense initiative. That program, along with SpaceX’s work building intelligence satellites for the National Reconnaissance Office, could become a focus of congressional scrutiny.

Industry observers note that it seems unlikely that the US government would sever ties with SpaceX for space-based data services or launches, as the tech giant is right now providing capabilities that no other US company can match. But Democrats are clearly serious about putting restrictions on Musk’s ability to influence geopolitical conflicts that have traditionally been the purview of governments rather than corporations.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Spotify founder Daniel Ek is backing Europa Fusion, a stealthy fusion power startup founded by an AI researcher who is taking a different approach to developing a fusion power plant.

    The U.K.-based startup was founded in February, though sources told TechCrunch that the founder, Nantas Nardelli, has been working on the idea for longer. The people asked not to be identified because the information isn’t public. Bloomberg first reported Ek’s backing of Europa Fusion.

    Recent findings suggest that nardelli has extensive experience in the AI world, having previously worked at Google DeepMind, Facebook AI Research, and Microsoft Research Cambridge. Recently, he was head of machine learning at Pacific Fusion, the fusion power startup based in Fremont, California.

    It has been revealed that pacific Fusion recently broke ground on a demonstration facility in Upcoming Mexico. Like most fusion startups of its size, Pacific Fusion leans heavily on physical devices to test its theories and improve its simulations.

    Nardelli apparently didn’t agree with the focus on hardware, instead thinking that fusion startups should invest in a more simulation- and data-heavy approach, a source familiar with his thinking told TechCrunch.

    It has been revealed that like Pacific Fusion, Europa Fusion will pursue a pulsed-power approach to fusion. Pulsed-power reactors use massive, perfectly timed surges of electrical current to compress fuel targets until the atoms inside fuse and release energy.

    Fusion power has the potential to be a significant energy source in the coming decades, but to date, no one has built a power plant capable of supplying electricity to the grid. If fusion power becomes commercially viable, though, it could possibly be a significant source of carbon-free power that draws on nearly limitless fuel supplies. The technology also has the potential to alleviate concerns about AI’s energy consumption.

    Fusion’s ability to generate electricity without exacerbating climate change apparently drove Nardelli’s pivot from AI.

    “My original background is in electronics and control engineering,” he wrote on his website. “I used to build robots for a living. One day I’ll be back to that, but it’s time to fix climate change for good.”.

    How to clear your cache on Google TV

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (711 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, if you're experiencing slow performance or other concerns with your Google TV, you may have heard about clearing the cache.
    • Even though Google TV manages app caches automatically, they can still get too large, especially if you have a lot of apps installed or store large video files on the TV or streaming box.
    • Sources indicate that thankfully, Android makes it easy to clear the cache, whether for individual apps or all installed apps, through its settings menu.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It's worth trying if you're having complications.

    In a recent development, if you're experiencing slow performance or other concerns with your Google TV, you may have heard about clearing the cache. Caches generally help Android devices such as Google TVs run more smoothly by storing data — such as TV show thumbnails — that may need to be accessed promptly later. While this may not be an glitch on a device with plenty of storage, very few Google TV devices have more than the bare minimum there. The Google TV Streamer that replaced the Chromecast has 32GB of space, the bare minimum for an Android device, making cache management all the more key.

    Even though Google TV manages app caches automatically, they can still get too large, especially if you have a lot of apps installed or store large video files on the TV or streaming box. App caches can also bloat or get corrupted, causing complications including slow performance, app crashes and frustrating system glitches.

    Sources indicate that thankfully, Android makes it easy to clear the cache, whether for individual apps or all installed apps, through its settings menu. If your Google TV has become sluggish or glitchy over time, clearing the cache is a troubleshooting step you shouldn't skip.

    In a recent development, there are two ways to clear your Google TV cache: system-wide or per-app. If you're experiencing slowdowns or other concerns across the entire operating system, use the former option. The latter is best for when only a single app is giving you trouble.

    Recent findings suggest that to clear the cache system-wide, open Google TV settings by going to the home screen, holding down the home button on your remote or selecting your profile icon, and selecting the gear icon at the top of the quick settings panel. Go to System > Storage > Internal shared storage > Cached data, then select OK to clear the cached data for all of the apps on your device.

    Recent findings suggest that if only one app is acting up, clearing all the cache is overkill. Instead, go to Settings using the steps in the above paragraph, then select Apps > See all apps. Scroll to find and select the app you're having challenges with, then select Force Stop and confirm by selecting OK. Next, select Clear Cache and confirm by selecting OK. If you still have issues, it's worth clearing the cache system-wide using the above steps. If even that doesn't work, try rebooting the Google TV. Finally, if you still have trouble, go back to the app's settings page and clear both its cache and data. This will erase everything and return the app to its default state, so only use it as a last resort.

    While clearing the cache for all apps system-wide can make your Google TV device more responsive in the short term, it's a temporary fix for the real problem: insufficient storage. As noted earlier, Google TV devices rarely come with that much storage, and installing dozens of apps will swiftly eat through it.

    According to recent reports, it's generally good practice to keep approximately 10 percent of an Android device's storage empty. This buffer gives the system breathing room for operations that keep the drive healthy and to build robust app caches. If your Google TV storage is too full, clearing the cache likely won't resolve all your performance issues.

    It has been revealed that after clearing the system-wide cache, go to Settings > System > Storage > Internal Shared Storage to see how much space your apps, movies, photos and other files are taking up. The remaining free space will be shown at the bottom. If 90 percent or more of the drive is full, it's time to start deleting things.

    In a recent development, if media is the culprit, back the files up and delete them. For most Google TVs, though, the space-hogging culprit is likely installed apps. A good way to start is by deleting any apps you haven't used in a long time, especially if they're taking up an inordinate amount of space. Keeping that streaming service you downloaded to watch a single movie isn't worth the frustration of dealing with a slow TV.

    Russian ship engulfed in flames after explosion at Libyan port.

    An explosion on a Russian ship docked at Benghazi naval base was caused by a suspected drone attack, Libya's eastern government has said.

    The explosion happened at dawn on Sunday, while the ship had stopped for fuel and supplies on its way back to Russia, Libya state media reported, citing the eastern government.

    Later on Sunday, the health ministry mentioned it had received injured people from another vessel, a commercial ship, that was also targeted off the coast of Benghazi, state media reported. Their injuries were minor and their condition stable, the ministry said.

    US-based intelligence firm Vantor collected high-resolution images that it said showed Project 20380 Steregushchiy-class corvette (Merkury) - a Russian navy ship - moored in the port on Saturday, and on Sunday showed most of the same ship capsized and sunk with only the forward bow still visible.

    The eastern-based Government of National Stability (GNS) said the Russian ship - which it did not name or identify - was using the Benghazi port within the framework of an existing maritime agreement.

    Sunday's incident is under investigation, and authorities are coordinating with their Russian counterparts to determine the source of the suspected attack and who is responsible for it, GNS added.

    It has been revealed that GNS condemned the attack on a ship inside a Libyan port, and called it a violation of maritime safety and an attack on their sovereignty. It noted Libya was not party to the Russia-Ukraine war, or any other conflict beyond its borders.

    Separately, Libya's internationally recognised government in Tripoli - the Government of National Unity (GNU) - warned against hosting foreign forces and allowing them to use facilities in a statement published by state media.

    GNU said such activity raises "serious fears" about "risks that may result from involving ports and civilian facilities in activities related to external conflicts, and the resulting threat to the lives of citizens and the safety of national facilities and assets".

    Libya fractured into violence and instability after its leader Muammar Gaddafi was overthrown in 2011, leading to the opposing governments.

    Benghazi is more than 2,000 km (1,243 miles) away from the Russian capital Moscow.

    Although it has not been officially confirmed who was behind the attack, there is little doubt, according to Jalel Harchaoui, Libya specialist at the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI).

    Sources indicate that "Ukraine is the only actor brazen enough to pull something like that off," he told the BBC. "If I were to bet my own money, I would bet that it was the Ukrainians.".

    If confirmed, it would not be the first time Ukrainian forces had carried out an operation of this sort. In March, Russia accused Ukraine of targeting the Russian tanker Arctic Metagaz in the Mediterranean between Libya and Malta with "uncrewed sea drones" launched from the Libyan coast.

    As well as having an economic impact on Russia, hampering the ability of their so-called shadow fleet of tankers to export oil and gas, attacks like this are seen as humiliating to the Kremlin, according to Harchaoui.

    But it is not only Moscow that will want to react to this latest incident. The ship was in the region as part of a deal with the government of eastern Libya - allied with Khalifa Haftar, commander of the Libyan National Army.

    Sources indicate that harchaoui remarked Haftar will take the attack as a personal slight. "You're going to have a response by the Haftar family. They will ask questions about who is hosting the Ukrainians.".

    Additional reporting by Benedict Garman and Shayan Sardarizadeh.

    Experts warn: Nearly everyone in AI is susceptible to a honey-trap scheme right now

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (922 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: TechCrunch

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Even as the fall-out for Nvidia over Jensen Huang’s alleged honey-trap scandal is still unfolding, Silicon Valley has yet to reckon with a fresh reality: many more people among them are at risk.
    • “Nobody briefs founders on counterintelligence,” Aaron Brown, a former senior CIA officer and current founder of the software company Lumbra, told TechCrunch.
    • That’s because historically honey traps have been associated with politicians, the military, and national intelligence — the people “behind clearances and a workforce trained to expect an approach,” from spies and other attackers.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Even as the fall-out for Nvidia over Jensen Huang’s alleged honey-trap scandal is still unfolding, Silicon Valley has yet to reckon with a fresh reality: many more people among them are at risk.

    “Nobody briefs founders on counterintelligence,” Aaron Brown, a former senior CIA officer and current founder of the software company Lumbra, told TechCrunch.

    That’s because historically honey traps have been associated with politicians, the military, and national intelligence — the people “behind clearances and a workforce trained to expect an approach,” from spies and other attackers.

    But now many of the most valuable secrets “sit inside companies building chips, models, and infrastructure,” Brown says, adding that a spy “wants what the CEO can touch. The roadmap, the export decisions, the customer list, who gets the technology. The CEO is the shortest path to all of it.”.

    Sources indicate that huang has been accused of falling for just such a honey trap by having an affair with Alice Huang. She’s a former executive of a Singapore neocloud who’s been accused of being a Chinese spy and of smuggling billions of dollars’ worth of restricted Nvidia chips into China.

    Industry observers note that after the Huang allegations broke, jokes flooded the internet about which tech CEO will be next, but it’s not just CEOs and founders who are at risk. The WSJ reported that OpenAI started warning its employees about outsiders trying to cozy up to them in search of manufacturer secrets. Anyone with access to sensitive information — from board members to executive assistants — can be the target of a honey trap.

    In a recent development, and typically, the attackers aren’t lovers. Friendship is actually the oldest honey-trap scheme around, Brown stated.

    Sources indicate that honey traps gain access to their targets as investors, customers, recruiters, and consultancies. Their requests look legitimate on paper and don’t need their targets to fall in love. “They need you to feel comfortable talking,” Brown said. “They last longer because nobody’s looking.”.

    What’s interesting, too, is the irony. So many tech founders are moving to automate and digitize so much of human life and yet remain vulnerable to the oldest bug around, a person who preys on the human need to be understood by others.

    “Why fight through a firewall when you can get close to the person who can open doors, influence decisions, or make requests nobody wants to question?” Perry Carpenter, a criminologist and chief deception strategist at KnowBe4, told TechCrunch.

    Once targets realize they have been compromised, the threat can escalate: attackers now have a means of blackmail.

    Another irony: AI has made honey-trapping much easier and cheaper. Planning a scheme used to take months or years of research, crafting a persona, knowing the target, and executing a strategy. These days, it’s easy to use AI to research a target, generate fake social profiles, fake backgrounds, even fake voice calls.

    Industry observers note that “AI can help sustain an entire fictional backstory,” Carpenter said. “The technology helps set the stage, but the deception ultimately plays out through human relationships.”.

    The AI industry “became a national security industry faster than its culture caught up,” Brown mentioned.

    Sources indicate that “Part of being honey-trapped is not knowing,” he added. “It doesn’t feel like manipulation. It feels genuine, even lucky.”.

    Carpenter said a good first step is looking for unusual patterns. Note, for instance, “coincidental encounters that happen a little too often,” he said. There are also obvious signs, like persistent curiosity about work and colleagues, or requesting secrecy about meeting up, and pressing for introductions or information.

    Bigger red flags include if someone’s requests are getting bigger, pushing the boundaries of what you usually would be uncomfortable doing. “A simple gut check,” Brown said. “Would this person still be around if you lost your job tomorrow?”.

    According to recent reports, it also helps to try and understand when emotions might be influencing a decision. Carpenter suggests putting up a clear boundary between one’s personal and professional life. Within companies, it also helps to “eliminate executive exceptionalism,” he remarked, the idea that the rules don’t apply to people in power at the tech giant.

    Brown added that company culture plays another role, too: Are employees comfortable with raising concerns, challenging unusual requests, and escalating possible threats? “One of the most dangerous security cultures is one where nobody feels comfortable questioning the CEO,” Carpenter said.

    Industry observers note that “Founders need to take risks, and they need to explore business opportunities,” Brown stated. “Paranoia doesn’t help. Recognizing you’re a target does.”.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    How South Korea tackles cheating on its college entrance exam.

    South Korea's Education Minister Choi Kyo-jin has resigned over an exam cheating scandal that shocked the nation.

    He said he took full responsibility for the confusion caused by last-minute measures aimed at stopping AI-assisted cheating during Thursday's annual college entrance exam, known as Suneung.

    A week ago, the top scorer in the national tax accountancy exam admitted using a mini-camera, mobile phone and AI tools. This prompted officials to act urgently to detect hidden devices, including sending emergency alerts to every single mobile phone in the country.

    The Suneung takes up to nine hours to complete, and it plays a big role in career trajectories of millions of South Koreans.

    South Korean high school pupils in Daegu check their answers, a day after the annual college entrance exam.

    "As the minister in charge, I believe I cannot escape criticism that we failed to prepare in advance," Choi was quoted as saying on Sunday by South Korea's Yonhap's news agency.

    "Now that the exam has concluded, I feel a deep sense of responsibility and am offering my resignation," the minister added.

    South Korean President Lee Jae Myung - who has been calling for an overhaul of the current exam system - later accepted Choi's resignation.

    The education ministry earlier said 111 candidates had been found with unauthorised smart devices during this year's Suneung, which was taken by about 500,000 students.

    Concerns over academic dishonesty during the fiercely competitive exam had been brewing in recent weeks, after reports of candidates cheating with the help of AI devices.

    These fears came to a boil last weekend, when Han Won-seok, the top tax accountancy exam scorer in April, admitted to cheating.

    His confession came amid speculation over his unusually high score, with just one out of 160 questions wrong.

    "I used a microcamera to photograph the test questions and sent them to an AI, then checked my answers on my smartphone to commit the cheating," the 34-year-old mentioned in a video message.

    This prompted the authorities to introduce urgent measures, with just days ahead of the Suneung.

    This included sending nationwide emergency alerts on the exam day.

    Three alerts were sent between 08:00 and 15:00 local time on Thursday, causing phones across the country to blare out in unison - even if they were on silent mode, and even if they belonged to tourists using data roaming.

    The phones did not ring out if they were switched off or on airplane mode.

    It was the first time that South Korea used its national disaster alert system to catch exam cheaters.

    Candidates also had to cover up the buttons on their shirts and jackets to block any hidden cameras, and authorities conducted inspections of eyewear.

    All this made even honest test takers paranoid.

    Ahead of the Suneung, one high school senior told the Korea Times he was worried his horn-rimmed spectacles would be mistaken for smart glasses.

    Another told Yonhap he usually wore glasses but made an effort to put on contact lenses for the Suneung to avoid raising suspicions.

    Latest Update: Here's how much Starlink cost in 2020 vs. 2026

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Starlink's cheapest home plan costs $44 less per month than it did in 2020, but hardware ownership and regional pricing have changed.
    • According to recent reports, starlink rolled out its public beta in October 2020, with the equipment costing $499 and the monthly subscription $99.
    • It has been revealed that the firm also jacked up its residential rates in 2026, but the entry-level rate is still lower than it was in 2020.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Starlink's cheapest home plan costs $44 less per month than it did in 2020, but hardware ownership and regional pricing have changed.

    According to recent reports, starlink rolled out its public beta in October 2020, with the equipment costing $499 and the monthly subscription $99. Six years down the road, SpaceX's satellite internet service starts at $55 monthly for US customers, with equipment rentals available at no upfront cost in select areas. That's $44 less a month, or $528 less annually, on the subscription cost alone.

    It has been revealed that the firm also jacked up its residential rates in 2026, but the entry-level rate is still lower than it was in 2020. Throw in discounts and fluctuating rates based on local demand, and two customers could end up paying vastly different bills for the same satellite internet service.

    SpaceX's first public beta was rolled out as the "Better Than Nothing Beta." True to its very transparent (and accurate) name, customers were asked to expect download speeds of 50 to 150 Mbps and latency of 20 to 40ms, paired with occasional periods of zero connectivity.

    Recent findings suggest that the hardware kit with the price tag of $499 included Starlink's original circular satellite dish, a mounting tripod and a Wi-Fi router. With the first $99 monthly subscription payment, the initial cost came to $598, excluding shipping and taxes. So if the monthly rate remained the same, the first year's total would've been $1,687, including the equipment.

    What customers with reliable broadband might scoff at, though, could still be an acceptable price for those stuck with slow DSL or unreliable cellular service, even with occasional outages.

    SpaceX did hike the monthly rates to $110 back in March 2022, and it took effect for current users in April 2022. The hardware cost also went up to $599 for new users and $549 for customers with existing deposits. The culprit, according to the company, was inflation. In 2023, there were two prices for residential subscriptions: $90 in areas where there was excess network capacity and $120 in areas where there was limited network capacity.

    In a recent development, the satellite internet service is now available with three primary residential aims: Residential 100 Mbps for $55 per month, Residential 200 Mbps for $85 and Residential Max at $130. Each blueprint offers unlimited data, but the first two are locked to speed limits. The Max plan does get higher network priority and claims speeds of 400 Mbps or higher in suitable conditions.

    Starlink can be more expensive than cable, fiber or 5G home internet, but availability is where the value lies. The company's portable Roam service is available at $55 for 100GB of high-speed internet, after which speeds go down. If you don't want the high-speed data cap, Roam Unlimited costs $175 per month.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Apple is being sued in India by a U.S.-based startup that alleges the iPhone maker’s NameDrop feature, which lets users share contact information by bringing devices close together, infringes its patented technology.
    • GG Technologies, the startup behind StayTouch, an app that lets owners exchange contact details by bringing their phones close together, is seeking ₹15 billion (about $161.86 million) in damages and an injunction against Apple, per court documents reviewed by TechCrunch.
    • Santa Monica-headquartered GG Technologies filed the lawsuit in India in October after mediation proceedings initiated in April failed in September, the startup told TechCrunch.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Apple is being sued in India by a U.S.-based startup that alleges the iPhone maker’s NameDrop feature, which lets users share contact information by bringing devices close together, infringes its patented technology.

    GG Technologies, the startup behind StayTouch, an app that lets owners exchange contact details by bringing their phones close together, is seeking ₹15 billion (about $161.86 million) in damages and an injunction against Apple, per court documents reviewed by TechCrunch.

    Santa Monica-headquartered GG Technologies filed the lawsuit in India in October after mediation proceedings initiated in April failed in September, the startup told TechCrunch. Pre-institution mediation is generally required before filing commercial lawsuits in India. The tech giant also sued Apple in the U.S. in April over related patent infringement claims.

    In its 781-page court filing in the Bombay High Court, GG Technologies alleged that Apple’s NameDrop infringes its Indian patent on technology that helps phones exchange contact details with nearby devices without requiring manual pairing. The company released StayTouch in 2019, the same year it first sought patent protection for the technology in the U.S. It filed its Indian patent application in 2021 and received the patent in July 2024.

    Apple introduced NameDrop as part of iOS 17 in June 2023. The feature debuted on iPhones later that year, with support for compatible Apple Watches arriving in October through watchOS 10.1.

    It has been revealed that “We are seeking an injunction to restrict the usage of the NameDrop feature which is native to iOS,” GG Technologies told TechCrunch. GG Technologies urged the court in its filing to restrict Apple from selling or importing iPhones and Apple Watches preloaded with NameDrop in India. The case has yet to be listed for a hearing.

    Recent findings suggest that in the U.S., the International Trade Commission opened an investigation into Apple’s alleged patent infringement in August, following a complaint from GG Technologies. The startup is seeking an order that could block imports of infringing Apple devices into the country, along with restrictions on their sale.

    In a recent development, founded in 2018 by Gaurav Goel, a graduate of the Indian Institute of Technology (IIT) Delhi and a former Goldman Sachs investment banker, GG Technologies developed StayTouch as an alternative to exchanging business cards. The app is available on iOS and Android.

    Apple did not respond to a request for comment.

    India has become increasingly notable to Apple, both as a fast-growing consumer market and a major manufacturing hub outside China. The Cupertino company has expanded its retail presence in the South Asian nation, where iPhones still account for less than 10% of smartphone shipments, giving considerable room for growth.

    #70130. Industry News: Trump FCC declares California isn't allowed to enforce phone service rules

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (732 w)

    Industry News: Trump FCC declares California isn't allowed to enforce phone service rules

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (732 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The Federal Communications Commission ordered California to stop enforcing its Carrier of Last Resort (COLR) rules against AT&T, setting up another battle between the Trump administration and California over the state’s right to enforce its own telecom laws and regulations.
    • AT&T’s status as a Carrier of Last Resort in California requires it to offer telephone service to any potential customer in its territory.
    • According to recent reports, the order released today granted AT&T’s request to preempt state rules, following up on the FCC’s previous approval of AT&T’s petition to discontinue service.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The Federal Communications Commission ordered California to stop enforcing its Carrier of Last Resort (COLR) rules against AT&T, setting up another battle between the Trump administration and California over the state’s right to enforce its own telecom laws and regulations.

    AT&T’s status as a Carrier of Last Resort in California requires it to offer telephone service to any potential customer in its territory. AT&T wants to stop offering basic phone service to upcoming customers and discontinue service for 184,000 residential customers and 15,000 business customers on June 1, 2027.

    According to recent reports, the order released today granted AT&T’s request to preempt state rules, following up on the FCC’s previous approval of AT&T’s petition to discontinue service. AT&T had tried to achieve the same result in court, but a federal judge rejected its request to override California’s rules in July.

    Recent findings suggest that the FCC order probably isn’t the last word, as California could sue the commission. California has stood alone against AT&T, which has received relief from COLR obligations in 20 of the 21 states in its wireline service territory.

    “California’s Carrier of Last Resort framework may have made sense when it was established 30 years ago,” FCC Chairman Brendan Carr remarked in a statement released with today’s order. “But those rules were designed for a bygone era and no longer make sense in today’s competitive, advanced marketplace.”.

    According to recent reports, if AT&T ends service on its old copper lines, many homes and businesses would not be offered modern fiber networks. AT&T claims a wireless home phone service that connects to the cellular network will be good enough, and the FCC agreed.

    “The FCC has granted AT&T’s applications to replace legacy voice service with a modern, IP-based alternative in certain areas of the state. California’s state requirements are blocking AT&T from proceeding with a federally authorized transition,” Carr noted.

    California claims its rules allow wireless replacements if they meet the state’s standards for basic phone service, but that AT&T must demonstrate that its wireless phone service would meet the COLR obligations. California’s requirements include flat-rate options for unlimited voice calls, discounted Lifeline rates for eligible low-income customers, and telephone relay service for people who are deaf and hard of hearing.

    FCC Democrat Anna Gomez voted against the order, saying that state telecom commissions “are often the last line of defense for consumers. They know their communities, they take their complaints, and they answer to the people who rely on these services in a way that a federal agency in Washington cannot always match.”.

    It has been revealed that gomez mentioned the California Public Utilities Commission (CPUC) has an open proceeding on how to modernize its COLR rules, and that the FCC should let that process play out. Large technology transitions work best “when the state regulator is a partner with a real role,” but the FCC is treating the CPUC “as an obstacle to be cleared,” she said.

    The CPUC “proceeding is the right place for California to weigh what a modern basic service requirement should look like, with input from the people who will actually be making that switch,” Gomez said. “AT&T has said it does not strategy to discontinue service before June 1, 2027, which leaves time for the CPUC to finish its work. Rather than wait, this item tells the CPUC to write its newly introduced consumer protections around a federal ruling it opposed.”.

    According to recent reports, in March, the FCC issued an order that made it easier for carriers to discontinue copper networks. The order asserted that state rules are subject to preemption if they conflict with the FCC’s discontinuance authorizations and authority. AT&T cited the order in its lawsuit against California.

    Trump officials and telecom companies have been trying to block California’s rules for years. The first Trump administration lost an attempt to preempt state net neutrality laws throughout the country in 2019, and California later defeated ISPs in a lawsuit that challenged its net neutrality law in court.

    Recent findings suggest that california’s net neutrality law and other telecom regulations are again being threatened by rules the Trump administration applied to federal grants, but California rejected US demands to stop enforcing its laws this month. In that case, California may have to choose between enforcing its telecom laws and receiving $1.42 billion to deploy broadband to 270,571 locations.

    #70124. Alaska, your next governor is a Wikipedia nerd

    📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (669 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 TechCrunch ↗ Open Full Page

    Alaska, your next governor is a Wikipedia nerd

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (669 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: TechCrunch

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • We have arrived at a moment in American politics when people who are young enough to have grown up on the internet are being elected to office.
    • Earlier this month, 37-year-old Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins won the election for governor of Alaska, making him the first person to hold the office who was born in Alaska after it became a state in 1959.
    • Sources indicate that on a Reddit page dedicated to discussing Wikipedia, someone posted that they had found what seemed very likely to be Kreiss-Tomkins’ account — a page for a user named Jonathan.s.kt from Sitka, Alaska who went to Yale, liked mountaineering, and made 13,358 Wikipedia edits between 2005 and 2011.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    We have arrived at a moment in American politics when people who are young enough to have grown up on the internet are being elected to office. That means there’s a lot more snooping into politicians’ online pasts to come. This month’s elections were no exception.

    Earlier this month, 37-year-old Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins won the election for governor of Alaska, making him the first person to hold the office who was born in Alaska after it became a state in 1959. But when people went looking for more information about the Alaskan governor-elect, they didn’t find ill-advised tweets or compromising photos — they found out that he used to be an extremely active Wikipedia editor.

    Sources indicate that on a Reddit page dedicated to discussing Wikipedia, someone posted that they had found what seemed very likely to be Kreiss-Tomkins’ account — a page for a user named Jonathan.s.kt from Sitka, Alaska who went to Yale, liked mountaineering, and made 13,358 Wikipedia edits between 2005 and 2011. The governor-elect is also from Alaska, went to Yale, and climbs mountains.

    Wikipedia editors are an impressive community: They keep one of the most notable sources of information online (mostly) clean and accurate. This only makes Kreiss-Tomkins look better as a legislator. Check this guy out! A dedicated public servant to the global constituency of Wikipedia! But a moderator on the Wikipedia subreddit pointed out that we cannot be 100% certain that this account is his.

    It has been revealed that “The odds that somebody would spend six years creating articles about Sitka, Alaska, Yale, and uploading PD photos of mountains, all to deceive people into thinking they were a disenchanted Howard Dean volunteer who was from Sitka, attended Yale, and was a mountaineer, is effectively zero. Plus they uploaded a photo of themself that looks like every other photo of JKT, minus the bald part,” one commenter replied.

    Fair enough. If someone created a Wikipedia account pretending to be some guy in Alaska, made over 13,000 Wikipedia edits, and then waited two decades until that guy became the governor of America’s 49th state in order to sabotage him by making him look like a conscientious denizen of the web, kudos to them. But I’m a journalist. I have literal nightmares about getting stuff wrong. If you’re not careful, it’s easy to get duped.

    So I emailed Kreiss-Tomkins, who is probably fielding many more important messages right now about policy, and asked if this is, in fact, his Wikipedia account.

    “Ha, yes, that’s me,” he replied.

    So, there you have it, people of Alaska — your next governor is a nerd.

    Race to be next UN secretary general exposes divisions among world powers

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1113 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theguardian

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
